articles.title: ASML vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? - The Motley Fool
articles.summary: ASML vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?  The Motley Fool
articles.full_text:
Demand for advanced computing power links two of the chip industry's best-known companies. ASML Holding (ASML -1.69%) makes the lithography systems that chipmakers use to print circuits on silicon, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM -1.98%), known as TSMC, is a contract manufacturer that makes chips for other companies.
The two also work together. In a joint release in September, ASML and TSMC said they had formed an initiative to move High NA EUV lithography to larger photomasks, and that TSMC intends to use ASML's High NA technology in high-volume manufacturing for advanced nodes starting in 2030.
Investors often compare them because their businesses are closely linked, even though their financial profiles differ.
ASML & TSM: Performance Comparison
Key Financial Metrics
The case for ASML
ASML supplies chipmakers with lithography systems and related software and services used to print circuit patterns on silicon wafers. Its flagship products include Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) and Deep Ultraviolet (DUV) machines used to produce advanced chips. ASML says it is currently the world's only manufacturer of EUV lithography systems. According to ASML's 2025 annual report, four customers accounted for about 61% of ASML's 2025 net sales.
ASML reports its results in euros, and the annual figures here are approximate conversions to U.S. dollars. In 2025, revenue reached nearly $36.6 billion, up roughly 15.6% from the previous year. The company reported net income of about $10.8 billion for the period, resulting in a net margin of nearly 29.4%.
For the quarter ended June 28, 2026, ASML reported net sales of 9.3 billion euros and a gross margin of 54%. In July, it raised its 2026 outlook to total net sales of 43-45 billion euros.
Based on its December 2025 balance sheet, ASML's debt-to-equity ratio, calculated from total debt and shareholders' equity, is about 0.2x. This ratio compares total debt to shareholders' equity, indicating modest borrowing relative to shareholders' equity.
The current ratio, also calculated from the balance sheet, measures the ability to pay short-term obligations with assets expected to convert to cash within a year, and is roughly 1.3x. Free cash flow, which ASML calculates as operating cash flow minus purchases of property, plant, and equipment and intangible assets, was approximately $12.4 billion for the year.
The case for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing
TSMC operates as a pure-play foundry, meaning it manufactures chips for customers rather than designing its own. In 2025, it manufactured 12,682 products for 534 customers, with demand coming from markets such as high-performance computing and smartphones. Advanced technologies at 7 nanometers and below accounted for 74% of its 2025 wafer revenue.
TSMC reports its results in New Taiwan dollars, and the annual figures here are approximate conversions to U.S. dollars.
In 2025, revenue reached roughly $121.3 billion, up about 31.6% in New Taiwan dollars and 35.9% in U.S. dollars, according to TSMC. The company earned net income of about $54.7 billion, for a net margin of approximately 45.1%.
For the quarter ended June 30, 2026, TSMC reported revenue up 36% year over year in New Taiwan dollars, with a gross margin of 67.7%.
Based on TSMC's December 2025 balance sheet, I calculate a current ratio of roughly 2.5x to 2.6x, depending on which of TSMC's year-end statements is used. That means current assets are about two and a half times current liabilities.
The debt-to-equity ratio, calculated as interest-bearing debt divided by total equity, is approximately 0.2x, a modest level of debt relative to shareholder equity. Free cash flow, calculated by subtracting capital expenditures from operating cash flow, reached about NT$1.0 trillion, or approximately $32 billion at the converted rate, for the fiscal year.
Risk profile comparison
ASML's customer concentration is a risk, since a change in spending plans at any one of its four largest customers can move its results. Because its customers are chipmakers that decide when to add capacity, a slowdown in industry spending would reduce demand for its systems.
Export controls are another factor. ASML's annual report says, "Changes in export controls may have a material impact on our business for example on the sales volume, mix and timing," and China accounted for about 29% of its 2025 net sales in the geographic breakdown of its annual report.
According to its interim report, which attributes sales to the location of customers' facilities, China's share fell to about 16% of net sales in the first half of 2026.
TSMC's business requires heavy, continuing investment in factories and technology, with capital expenditures of about $40.9 billion in 2025, according to TSMC. Geopolitical risk is the other main concern, since the majority of its principal production facilities are in Taiwan. TSMC also faces competition from other foundries, including Intel (INTC -3.20%), which TSMC's chief executive described as a formidable competitor on the April 2026 earnings call, and Samsung Electronics (SSNLF +0.00%), which TrendForce estimates ranked second in foundry revenue in the second quarter of 2026.
TSMC's customer base is also concentrated at the top, as its annual report shows two customers accounted for 19% and 17% of 2025 net revenue. Demand for TSMC's chips also depends on its customers' end markets, including smartphones and consumer electronics, so weakness in those categories would affect sales.
Valuation comparison
TSMC has the lower forward P/E of the two in the table, and the two companies are close on price-to-sales. The P/S ratio measures a company's market value against its past twelve months of sales. The forward P/E compares the stock price to future earnings estimates.
| Metric | ASML | Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing | 
|---|---|---|
| Forward P/E | 42.8x | 28.0x | 
| P/S ratio | 18.2x | 17.5x | 
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
While TSMC looks like the better buy to me, I'd be a patient buyer, as shares of both companies have risen sharply over the past year and TSMC's production is concentrated in Taiwan.
My reasoning starts with the fact that each business depends on its customers. Both are concentrated.
TSMC's two largest customers accounted for about 36% of its 2025 net revenue, according to its annual report, and four customers accounted for about 61% of ASML's 2025 net sales. TSMC also serves 534 customers in total, so the business has a broader base beyond its largest accounts. ASML says it is currently the world's only manufacturer of EUV lithography systems, which is a strong foundation, though it also means a handful of chipmakers shape demand.
TSMC also carries the lower forward earnings multiple in the table, which adds to its appeal for me.
If I were buying, I'd start with a modest TSMC position and add to it over time, planning to hold for years. Sharp pullbacks can happen with both stocks, and if the business still looked sound after one, I'd treat it as a chance to add more.

articles.title: [News] CPU Price Hike Wave: Intel Reportedly Up to 20%, Qualcomm 10%, AMD May Join as TSMC Costs Climb - TrendForce
articles.summary: [News] CPU Price Hike Wave: Intel Reportedly Up to 20%, Qualcomm 10%, AMD May Join as TSMC Costs Climb  TrendForce
articles.full_text:
CPU price hikes are gaining momentum in October, fueled by growing demand for AI PCs and servers and rising advanced-node manufacturing costs. According to Commercial Times, Intel and Qualcomm have raised prices for certain processor products, while AMD is reportedly preparing adjustments of its own.
Foundry pricing is a key factor, with TSMC expected to raise its manufacturing prices further in 2027. According to Central News Agency, analysts forecast increases of 5% to 10% for advanced nodes, 10% to 15% for advanced packaging, and 3% to 5% for mature nodes, reflecting higher raw material and equipment costs.
Intel Raises High-End Panther Lake Prices by Up to 20%
Intel has raised processor prices three times since late last year. According to Commercial Times, the company reportedly introduced price adjustments across its product lines starting September 1, with high-end Panther Lake models seeing the largest increases of 15% to 20%, compared with 5% to 10% for Meteor Lake and Arrow Lake. The latest hikes do not apply to the entire Panther Lake lineup, but focus on models equipped with high-end GPU tiles.
As Commercial Times highlights, these Panther Lake models use high-end GPU tiles manufactured by TSMC on its N3E. Panther Lake adopts a heterogeneous integration architecture, combining these GPU tiles with CPU compute tiles produced on Intel’s own 18A.
Qualcomm Raises Chip Prices by 10%; AMD Reportedly Plans CPU Price Adjustments
Qualcomm has also moved to raise chip prices. According to Commercial Times, citing supply chain sources, the company increased prices for PC processor platforms including Snapdragon X and X2 Elite by approximately 10% starting in October. Industry sources note that Qualcomm’s expansion beyond smartphone SoCs into PCs, edge computing, and other high-performance computing markets, along with increasingly advanced CPU, GPU, and NPU specifications, is driving greater reliance on advanced nodes and packaging, adding to chip costs.
AMD is also reportedly preparing price adjustments for certain CPUs, although the magnitude, scope, and timing remain unconfirmed, according to Commercial Times. The company has already begun ramping production of its sixth-generation EPYC processors, codenamed Venice, on TSMC’s 2nm. Looking ahead, AMD plans to substantially increase chip supply in 2027. According to Reuters, CEO Lisa Su said on October 6 that the company is working with partners including TSMC to expand CPU and GPU production capacity to meet growing AI demand, highlighting its need for additional advanced wafer capacity.
Notebook CPU Supply Improves, but Rising Costs Continue to Pressure Brands
Higher CPU costs are adding to the challenges facing notebook manufacturers. According to TrendForce, CPU supply has improved significantly since 2Q26, allowing brands to gradually normalize procurement and production. However, continued increases in DRAM and SSD prices, alongside higher CPU costs, are putting further pressure on notebook makers.
TrendForce notes that as CPU shortages ease in 2H26, continued advance procurement by brands, earlier replacement purchases by consumers, and stable commercial demand are expected to support an upward revision to shipment forecasts. As a result, the decline in global notebook shipments for full-year 2026 is expected to narrow to 9.4% YoY.

The winning entry of the prestigious Small World in Motion microscopy competition has been disqualified after scientists raised concerns about its creation using artificial intelligence.
On 9 October, Nikon Instruments, which runs the competition, said in a statement that the winning video did not comply with competition rules. AI-generated videos are not permitted, according to the competition website.
The video was submitted by Ning Xu, an optical engineer at the National University of Singapore. It showed the movement of hair-like structures called cilia in the lungs and was awarded first place on 15 September. But in days, scientists noted on social-media platform LinkedIn that some features in the video seemed biologically implausible.
In response to those comments, Xu wrote on LinkedIn that his team had used an AI model in post-processing to enhance the visual presentation of the regions below the cilia “without making anatomical claims about what those rendered features represent”. These posts, which appeared under Nikon’s earlier announcement on LinkedIn that Xu had won the prize, have since been taken down.
On 25 September, a Nikon Small World spokesperson told Nature that the company was investigating the video. In its latest statement, Nikon Instruments said that after re-evaluating the video and supporting materials, and consulting the judging panel, it determined that the winning video did not comply with the competition rules. “This decision is based solely on the submitted video’s eligibility under the rules outlined for this competition. It should not be interpreted as a judgment of the entrant’s professional reputation, scientific contributions, or intent,” the company said.
Xu did not respond to Nature’s request for comment about Nikon’s decision to disqualify his entry. A spokesperson for the National University of Singapore said Ning Xu participated in the competition before he joined the university and the content of his submission is unrelated to his work there.

The New Dark Ages: The End of Reading and the Dawn of a Post-Literate SocietyJames Marriott Bodley Head (2026)
The thriller novelist Dan Brown writes books that some critics complain are for people who don’t read books. The journalist and former rare-book seller James Marriott has now written a book for people who read books about people who don’t. That must have been an interesting sales pitch. What’s next — a 3.5-hour-long radio documentary about declining attention spans?
People who read books should read this one. The New Dark Ages will make you feel both alarmed and a little smug. In Marriott’s telling, book readers are better-informed, happier people who contribute more to a rational rules- and evidence-based society and help to safeguard the rights and principles of liberal democracy. Even those who read Dan Brown’s books? Absolutely.
Reading, even airport thrillers, forces people to engage with the world and other people in ways that other forms of media simply do not require. Despite the rise of technology, reading remains the best way to experience being a person other than ourselves, Marriott says. “Cinema, video games, television: for all their virtues, these art forms are hopelessly trapped in the exterior world of surfaces.”
This short, spirited work is a love letter to the written word, penned with the heartfelt and passionate language of a jilted spouse. “Not everything that is important or true can be said simply,” says Marriott, but he seems to have managed just fine.
Race for attention
Indeed, for a work that exalts literacy because it enables the reliable communication of complex ideas, The New Dark Ages presents a straightforward premise. Reading built the modern world, and helped to create science, democracy and reason.
But books are now dying, and as reading declines, so does the ability to think rationally. As a consequence, reasoned debate is on the slide in politics and much of public life.
If books are dying, then nobody told the people who write them, who between them are publishing more volumes year-on-year. The problem, Marriott says, is that books that sell, and are presumably read, are mostly the ‘wrong’ types — self-help, romance, detective stories and young-adult fiction, whereas sales of books about economics, current affairs and politics have fallen sharply.
There is better news for popular-science authors. In May, the Royal Society declared the past two decades a golden age for the genre, with sales soaring from 1.2 million books a year in 2000 to a peak of more than 5 million in 2019. By 2024, the total figure had dropped to 2.9 million but it was spread across an impressive 20,000 titles — about quadruple the number reported for 2000.
Books are getting simpler, Marriott says, with shorter sentences that make them easier to read. That means people don’t have to concentrate as much as he did as a teenager when he picked “uncomprehendingly” through the pages of Fyodor Dostoevsky — an exercise that taught him a valuable lesson.
“To discover the things that really enrich us we have to pay attention. We have to patiently endure our initial sensations of bafflement and annoyance ... until what seemed off-puttingly weird and wrong reveals itself to us as life-enrichingly true and profound.”
Generations of readers have struggled with Dostoevsky. So, what is different now? What is driving what Marriott labels as the Great Simplification, which leaves today’s teenagers and adults unwilling or unable to put in the required effort and levels of concentration? Why do teachers complain that their students can no longer make sense of the opening paragraphs of Charles Dickens’s Bleak House and other curriculum classics? The answer is in your pocket, your bag or, more likely, in your hand.
The smartphone, he writes, took the lure of television as a diversion from the written word and spread it across 24 hours, offering constant, instant and unfiltered access to content that is “pathetically ill-equipped to speak to the deeper human need for curiosity, learning, narrative, close attention and artistic fulfilment”.
Dense sentences, and the concentration and time required to decode and appreciate them, simply cannot compete with the addictive ever-present series of notifications and instant ‘reward’ of messages, hot takes and videos that are presented as entertainment but serve mostly as distraction.
Dickens could write hundreds of pages of sprawling digressive clauses, playful linguistic excursions and hyperactive minor characters, Marriott reflects, only because there was nothing more interesting for nineteenth-century readers to do. “Dickens wrote in the reasonable belief that Little Dorrit or Bleak House or Great Expectations might be the most absorbing entertainment in your house,” he says. “No modern author can write with that confidence.”
Threat to literacy
Those who shun reading because of its complexity and the amount of cognitive load it requires have nothing to fear from The New Dark Ages. I fell through its 170 pages in a couple of enjoyable hours. Marriott, now a newspaper columnist, likes pithy phrases and has the enviable knack of predicting and answering the questions that arise in the reader’s mind, without being asked. (Although I did need to look up the word periphrastic and, on learning what it meant, wondered if I was missing a joke — it means ‘wordy’.)
And a note to those shaking their heads and saying that they read on their smartphone, including maybe even this article, or his book: Marriott sees you.

articles.summary: Nvidia reportedly ends GeForce RTX 5090 graphics card production  GamesIndustry.bizNVIDIA Reportedly Ending the RTX 5090, Reserves GB202 Silicon for Workstation GPUs  TechPowerUpNvidia reportedly halts GeForce RTX 5090 production in favor of AI data center and professional GPUs — impending supply drought expected to drive up prices, RTX 5080 24GB rumored as new gaming flagship  Tom's HardwareNvidia Might Kill the RTX 5090 and Replace It With a 24GB RTX 5080 &nb...
articles.full_text:
Nvidia has reportedly stopped manufacturing the GeForce RTX 5090, including the D variants made for the Chinese market.
The claim comes from a leaked notice from an unnamed factory, shared by leaker @hongxing2020 and reported by Tom's Hardware. A second leaker, @Zed__Wang, reportedly backed the claim, saying the GB202 chip behind the RTX 5090 will only go into data center and professional cards from now on.
"According to a notification from the factory, Nvidia will no longer manufacture any RTX 5090 models, including the D variants," the message from @hongxing2020 reads. "Going forward, the highest-end GeForce graphics card will be the RTX 5080 24GB, while the RTX 5080 16GB version will be discontinued. Please spread the word."
Nvidia has not announced the change, and Tom's Hardware said the company had not responded to its request for comment.
An RTX 50 Super refresh, rumored to include a 24GB RTX 5080 Super, has reportedly been delayed by memory supply constraints, according to Tom's Hardware.
Rumors put the arrival of Nvidia's Rubin-based RTX 60-series at late 2027 at the earliest, and possibly 2028.
The industry-wide memory shortage has already affected other hardware. GamesIndustry.biz previously reported that Sony could delay the PS6 to 2028 or 2029 because of the crisis, Valve said it is limited by memory capacity, and Xbox warned memory costs would affect Project Helix's pricing and availability.

China struggles to shift tech firms away from Nvidia chips
Huawei says its Ascend chips now outsell Nvidia in China, but the country's top AI labs still lean on Nvidia hardware for model training
China wants its tech giants to run on homegrown silicon. Its top AI developers keep reaching for Nvidia anyway.
That tension sits at the center of Beijing’s push for semiconductor self-sufficiency. US export controls have made the effort urgent, and the gap between selling chips and changing habits is proving wider than policymakers might like.
Huawei is winning on volume, not on habits
Huawei, China’s leading domestic chip player, claims its Ascend AI chips have outsold Nvidia within China as of October 2026. For a company operating under heavy US restrictions, that is a notable milestone.
Eric Xu, Huawei’s rotating chairman, has framed the company’s pitch around dependable domestic supply rather than raw peak performance. The argument is simple: a chip you can actually buy beats a faster one you might not be allowed to get.
Many of China’s leading AI developers still rely on Nvidia hardware to train advanced large language models, the expensive, compute-hungry process of building an AI system from scratch.
DeepSeek offers the clearest example. The company plans to deploy at least 160,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT chips for inference, while keeping Nvidia hardware for its training workloads.
The software moat nobody can chip away at quickly
The stickiness comes down to software. Nvidia’s CUDA platform is the toolkit that developers use to write code that runs efficiently on Nvidia chips, and it has become deeply entrenched across the AI industry.

Huawei offers its own alternative, called CANN. A transition for training workloads is predicted to carry roughly 50% higher costs and time.
Inference deployments appear to be rolling out with more agility, which helps explain why Huawei’s sales numbers can climb even as Nvidia keeps its foothold at the top end.
Washington’s controls are shaping the board
All of this plays out against tight US restrictions on advanced chip exports to China. Enforcement has teeth. US authorities have arrested individuals involved in smuggling Nvidia chips into China, with cases still ongoing as of October 2026.
At the same time, Washington has granted limited approvals for certain Nvidia models despite the broader restrictions. The result is a patchwork: some Nvidia hardware moves legally, some moves illegally, and Chinese firms plan around the uncertainty of both.
What the market share math could look like
The projections are striking. Domestic AI chipmakers could capture approximately 50% of China’s AI accelerator market by 2026.
Nvidia’s share, meanwhile, may fall to around 8% in 2026, down from about 40% in 2025. Both things can be true at once: Nvidia could lose most of the unit volume in China while still powering a disproportionate share of the country’s frontier model training.
What this means
For Nvidia, the risk is less about one quarter’s revenue and more about the long game. China has been a lucrative AI market, and losing its dominant position there could ripple through the company’s global strategy and profitability.
For Huawei, winning inference is a meaningful foothold. Winning training, where switching costs are highest and performance matters most, is the harder prize, and the source of Nvidia’s remaining leverage.
Investors watching the sector should track a few signals. First, whether more top Chinese labs announce training runs on domestic hardware, which would indicate the CUDA moat is narrowing where it counts. Second, how Washington handles its limited Nvidia approvals going forward. Tighter rules would accelerate the shift to Huawei, while looser ones could give Chinese labs a reason to stay put. Third, whether the projected collapse in Nvidia’s China share actually materializes in 2026. A drop from about 40% to around 8% would reshape not just one company’s China business but the broader map of global semiconductor supply chains.

articles.title: ARDD 2026 Signals a New Era for Longevity Biotechnology as Frontier AI, Big Pharma, and Scientific Pioneers Converge at Harvard - Insilico Medicine
articles.summary: ARDD 2026 Signals a New Era for Longevity Biotechnology as Frontier AI, Big Pharma, and Scientific Pioneers Converge at Harvard  Insilico Medicine
articles.full_text:
The convergence of frontier artificial intelligence, large-scale biological data, and pharmaceutical innovation is opening new possibilities for understanding human aging, predicting disease, and developing interventions that could extend healthy human lifespan. At the 13th Aging Research and Drug Discovery (ARDD) meeting, held October 1–3 at Harvard University’s David Rubenstein Treehouse, leaders from across biotechnology, global pharmaceutical companies, academia, and investment gathered to explore how these rapidly advancing capabilities are reshaping the future of longevity science.
Founded in 2014 by Alex Zhavoronkov, PhD, Founder and Co-CEO of Insilico Medicine, ARDD made its North American debut in Boston following years of growth in Europe. What began as an academically focused scientific gathering has evolved into a global forum connecting fundamental aging biology with the computational power, industrial capabilities, and investment needed to advance a new generation of longevity technologies.
This year’s discussions highlighted an emerging inflection point for the field: the ability to integrate high-dimensional biological data, generative AI, virtual cell models, and increasingly sophisticated experimental systems to investigate aging at a scale and level of complexity previously beyond reach. Rather than treating aging solely as a collection of individual diseases and biological mechanisms, researchers are developing new approaches to model interconnected biological processes, identify opportunities for intervention, and ultimately translate these insights into measurable improvements in human health.
“The convergence we witnessed at ARDD 2026 represents a remarkable moment for longevity biotechnology,” said Alex Zhavoronkov, PhD, Founder and Co-CEO of Insilico Medicine and Co-Chair of ARDD. “We are seeing frontier AI, increasingly sophisticated biological models, and unprecedented volumes of human data begin to converge with the scientific and industrial capabilities needed to act on these insights. From virtual cells and biological world models to next-generation therapeutics, we are moving toward a future where aging can be studied and potentially intervened upon with far greater precision. The opportunity extends well beyond any single drug or technology. We are witnessing the emergence of an entirely new scientific and industrial frontier.”
Regulatory Spotlight: From HHS Health Policy Shifts to FDA Function-Based Approvals
Longevity therapeutics have long moved beyond the lab, yet the market faces a stark reality: peptides, supplements, and biological age tests are marketed directly to consumers, most without passing rigorous clinical validation. In a landmark milestone for the conference, senior officials from the US regulatory took the stage for the first time, delivering high-level keynotes and leading panel discussions to map out an actionable regulatory framework for longevity therapeutics.
According to Admiral Brian Christine, Assistant Secretary for Health at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), health policy must shift from reactively treating individual diseases to proactively preserving health and extending healthspan. He emphasized that targeting the biology of aging provides a unique opportunity to delay multiple age-related conditions at once. Under the HHS "Make America Healthy Again" framework, the government aims to break down agency silos among the NIH, FDA, and CDC, fund rigorous clinical trials, develop predictive biomarkers for functional outcomes, and rapidly translate research into clinical practice.
Addressing the central challenge of measuring endpoints for therapeutics targeting multiple age-related declines at once, the FDA sent a delegation of four representatives, presenting a pragmatic stance that progress in longevity therapeutics does not hinge on defining aging as a disease; rather, validated, function-based endpoints and shared data are the true path forward. CDER drug evaluation leaders revealed that the FDA's upcoming Regulatory Science Priority Areas document will officially include "aging and longevity," which formally incorporates longevity into the agency's strategic priorities even though the timeline remains unannounced.
During the policy panel moderated by ARPA-H, CDER officials outlined two viable approval pathways: demonstrating efficacy across two or three distinct age-related diseases, or targeting a broad aging indication measured by composite endpoints across functional domains like cognition, frailty, and vision. Crucially, regulators emphasized a strict "evidence ladder" for biomarkers, clarifying that predictive markers are not surrogates until proven to respond to treatment, map to risk reduction, and reproduce across interventional trials. While fully validated surrogates support traditional approval, "reasonably likely" surrogates can unlock accelerated approval pathways backed by confirmatory trials.
As Steven Kozlowski, FDA Chief Scientist noted, identifying shared underlying mechanisms across multiple chronic diseases remains the primary goal, offering a roadmap built on robust, longitudinal human data rather than theoretical claims.
Big Pharma Leans In: Bridging Geroscience and Disease Indications Through Hard Clinical Data
Pharmaceutical executives and R&D leaders from the world's top global biopharmaceutical companies outlined a pragmatic entry point for longevity therapeutics: securing initial regulatory approval in a defined age-related indication while systematically gathering aging biomarker data along the way. 
Fiona Marshall and Sophie Lemire-Brachat from Novartis noted that in addressing the clinical limitations of single-target regenerative therapies, Novartis is shifting its R&D strategy toward a systems-based approach centered on longitudinal human data (e.g., Data42, Our Future Health) and resilience biology, backed by a newly established Diseases of Aging and Regenerative Medicine department. Novartis emphasizes that its goal is not an "aging" approval, but rather to target specific aging-driven diseases and incorporate aging-relevant secondary or exploratory endpoints, while utilizing AI predictive models to balance efficacy against safety risks.
Parallel clinical and biomarker advances from Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, and AstraZeneca further illustrated how large-scale datasets are validating geroscience-derived interventions.

articles.title: StockWatch: Caribou Plunges as It Pursues Strategic Alternatives - Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News
articles.summary: StockWatch: Caribou Plunges as It Pursues Strategic Alternatives  Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News
articles.full_text:
Caribou Biosciences (Nasdaq: CRBU), whose co-founders include Jennifer Doudna, PhD, capped a one-year 83% freefall of its stock after announcing plans to evaluate strategic alternatives, as investors responded with a selloff that sent shares of the CRISPR genome-editing cell therapy developer plunging 62% this past week.
Caribou announced plans to carry out an unspecified “substantial” reduction of its workforce—which numbered 97 people as of February 27, according to its most recent Form 10-K Annual report, filed March 5—as well as a halt to trials of its two clinical-phase pipeline candidates, both allogeneic chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy programs, and other cost reduction measures also yet to be specified.
“Caribou’s story has taken a heartbreaking turn,” co-founder, president, and CEO Rachel Haurwitz, PhD, posted on LinkedIn, announcing the company’s strategic review. “This decision is not a loss of belief in our science, our clinical data, or what these programs could mean for patients. It reflects the difficult reality that the current financing environment for allogeneic CAR T-cell therapies has made it impossible to secure the capital required to responsibly advance them.”
Haurwitz co-established Caribou in 2011 along with Doudna and two other co-founders: Martin Jínek, PhD, a former postdoctoral fellow in Doudna’s lab, now at the University of Zurich, who led the seminal 2012 study leading to the Nobel Prize; and James Berger, PhD, professor in the department of biophysics and biophysical chemistry at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine.
Caribou became operational in 2012, which would make it the oldest CRISPR therapeutics company as far as Haurwitz could recall in a 2021 interview. That year, Caribou went public through an upsized initial public offering (IPO) that raised $321 million in aggregate net proceeds after deducting underwriting discounts and commissions and other offering expenses. Caribou sold 21.85 million shares at an IPO price of $16 a share, up from earlier plans to sell 13.5 million shares.
Two years later, Haurwitz shared with GEN her journey from graduate student in Doudna’s lab to launching a biotech start-up: “This is the only job I’ve ever had!”
Trials halted
As a result of the strategic review, Caribou has halted trials of vispacabtagene regedleucel (vispa-cel, formerly CB-010) a treatment for relapsed or refractory (r/r) B cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Caribou has said vispa-cel is the first allogeneic CAR T-cell therapy “to our knowledge” that has reached the clinic with a PD-1 knockout, a genome-editing strategy designed to improve antitumor activity by limiting premature CAR T-cell exhaustion.
To manufacture vispa-cel, Caribou applies Cas9 hybrid RNA-DNA guide or “chardonnay” (chRDNA) to make three edits: A knockout of the TRAC gene to remove the T cell receptor; a site-specific insertion of an anti-CD19 CAR into the TRAC gene; and a knockout of PD-1.
Also halted were clinical studies of CB-011, an allogeneic anti-BCMA CAR-T cell therapy for the treatment of patients with r/r multiple myeloma (RRMM). To manufacture CB-011, Caribou uses Cas12a chRDNAs designed to direct precise genome editing, in order to make four edits:
- A knockout of the TRAC gene to remove the T-cell receptor
- A site-specific insertion of a humanized anti-BCMA CAR into the TRAC gene
- A site-specific insertion of a gene encoding a B2M–HLA-E-peptide fusion into the B2M gene
- The resulting knockout of the endogenous B2M
“This method simultaneously eliminates endogenous HLA class I presentation on the surface of the CAR T cells and expresses HLA-E, a minor HLA class I antigen, to blunt both T and NK cell-mediated rejection of the CAR T-cell therapy by the patient’s immune system,” Caribou explained on its website.
Strategic pivot
The development of CB-011 and vispa-cel followed a strategic pivot by Caribou from a platform company for biopharma partners applying genome editing in research or product development, to a developer of genome-edited therapies based on its own next-generation CRISPR technology.
While that pivot has generated positive data readouts, it has not shielded Caribou from the financial challenges faced by numerous gene-edited therapy developers. In April 2025, Caribou chopped its workforce by 32% and pruned its pipeline by ending all preclinical research, the Phase I GALLOP trial (NCT06752876) of vispa-cel in lupus (before the first patient could be dosed), and development of CB-012, including the Phase I AMpLify trial (NCT06128044) assessing the candidate in relapsed or refractory acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
“It was really about right sizing the organization relative to our focused priorities,” Haurwitz explained last year in an interview. Asked how hopeful she was about an improving economic environment over the next 12 months, she replied: “I remain a believer and I remain an optimist. I’d probably be in the wrong job in the wrong line of work if I weren’t.”
“I certainly think for the work that we are doing, I continue to fully believe that doing right by patients is the North Star, because business success falls out from that in terms of nearer term clinical catalysts and opportunities that come from doing right by patients. And longer-term commercial opportunity also comes from doing right by patients,” Haurwitz added.
Caribou has retained Wedbush Securities as its exclusive financial advisor to assist in evaluating strategic options.
Caribou announced its pursuit of strategic alternatives after the closure of financial markets on October 6. The following day, Caribou shares began three days of stock declines, nosediving 46% from $1.14 to 62 cents. Those shares tumbled another 22% Thursday to 48 cents, but closed Friday with another 4% decline, finishing the week at 46 cents.
Cash crunch
Daina M. Graybosch, PhD, senior managing director, immuno-oncology and a senior research analyst with Leerink Partners, reported in a research note that Caribou was facing an increasingly pressing cash crunch at a time when the company needed significant capital to fund its planned Phase III ANTLER-3 trial, designed to assess vispa-cel in second-line auto-CAR T ineligible diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL).
Caribou never enrolled patients in the pivotal study, though it reached agreement with the FDA in May on a design for the trial, which was expected to be a randomized, controlled clinical study enrolling approximately 250 CD19-naïve second line (2L) large B cell lymphoma patients ineligible for transplant and not candidates or not eligible for autologous CAR T-cell therapy.
“We are sympathetic to management’s stated rationale for exploring strategic alternatives,” Graybosch commented. “Evidently, investors were unwilling to fund the trial on what would have been highly dilutive terms, especially in the context of lingering clinical risk and uncertainty around the strength of vispa-cel’s Ph[ase I/II] outcomes and partial HLA-matching strategy, as well as substantial in- and out-of-class competition.”
That competition, she wrote, included epcoritamab, a bispecific T-cell engager (BiTE) therapy already marketed as Epkinly® by Genmab (Nasdaq Copenhagen and Nasdaq: GMAB) and AbbVie (NYSE: ABBV).
On October 5—the day before Caribou’s strategic alternatives announcement—Genmab and AbbVie reported positive topline data from the Phase III EPCORE DLBCL-2 trial (NCT05578976) showing that the combination of epcoritamab, rituximab, the corticosteroid prednisone, and three chemotherapy drugs showed statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in progression-free survival (PFS) in frontline diagnosed DLBCL patients.
The combination therapy, nicknamed R-CHOP, consists of rituximab—the CD20-directed cytolytic antibody marketed by Genentech, a member of the Roche Group (SIX Swiss: RO and ROP) and Biogen (Nasdaq: BIIB) as Rituxan®—plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin hydrochloride, vincristine, and prednisone. In DLBCL patients with an International Prognostic Index (IPI) score of 2 to 5, R-CHOP reduced the risk of disease progression or death by 51% (HR 0.49 [95% CI 0.36, 0.67]; p-value < 0.0001).
“Interesting” timing
“The timing of [Caribou’s] initiative is interesting,” Graybosch observed. “We believe there is enhanced strategic value and clinical rationale for allogeneic cell therapies in a world where TCEs [T-cell engagers] become entrenched in the 1L [first-line] setting.”
As for CB-011, it began development much earlier than vispa-cel, “with an appreciably more challenging competitive setup in RRMM, where we saw elevated clinical risk for its post-BCMA therapy development path due to potential efficacy-compromising loss-of-antigen,” the Leerink Partners analyst added.
Single target allogeneic BCMA CAR-T treatments have posed a potential risk of RRMM relapse through antigen loss as myeloma cells mutate or downregulate BCMA to evade the CAR T cells. To minimize that risk, Caribou designed its Phase I CaMMouflage trial (NCT05722418) to limit the therapy dosing to BCMA-naïve patients—an approach that proved successful when the company last year announced positive data from a 12-patient, BCMA-naïve cohort showing a 92% overall response rate (11/12 patients), a 75% or greater complete response rate (9/12), and 91% minimal residual disease (MRD) negativity (10/11 evaluable patients).
To avoid the risk of antigen loss, several developers of allogeneic BCMA CAR-Ts have designed dual targeting CAR Ts. For example, Allogene Therapeutics (Nasdaq: ALLO) is developing ALLO-329, which targets CD19 on B cells and CD70 on activated T cells. ALLO-329 generated positive preclinical data in April, with a data update from the Phase I RESOLUTION trial (NCT07085104) expected later in Q4.

articles.title: NVIDIA Readies Continent-Scale AI Factories at OCP Summit 2026: Spectrum-XGS Debuts Tonight - Tech Times
articles.summary: NVIDIA Readies Continent-Scale AI Factories at OCP Summit 2026: Spectrum-XGS Debuts Tonight  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
Tonight in San Jose, Ian Buck — the NVIDIA vice president who built CUDA two decades ago and in doing so handed every deep-learning researcher on earth a practical on-ramp — will tell data-center architects how to build an AI factory that spans continents. His keynote at OCP 2026, scheduled for 5:45 PM PT at the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, is expected to center on four platform pillars NVIDIA has been assembling since January: the Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, the Vera CPU, the Spectrum-XGS scale-across network, and the DSX factory management suite. Of the four, Spectrum-XGS carries the largest structural implication — one the industry is only beginning to price in: for the first time, geography stops being an AI factory constraint.
The summit, now sold out at 7,000 to 9,000 attendees and running October 12–15, is the premier venue for the open hardware ecosystem that now supplies most of the world's hyperscale compute. Buck's session — formally titled "AI Factories at Scale: Advancing Open Infrastructure for Agentic AI" — is one of more than 22 conference sessions the event will host across four days.
Ian Buck: Architecture's Constants Change With CUDA, and Now With Spectrum-XGS
Ian Buck joined NVIDIA in 2004 after completing a PhD at Stanford, where his work on the Brook streaming language — described in Buck's Stanford dissertation on streaming — laid the conceptual groundwork for general-purpose GPU computing. As NVIDIA's vice president of Hyperscale and HPC, he has led the company's GPU computing strategy for more than twenty years, overseeing the period in which the NVIDIA CUDA unified computing platform became the de facto programming model for AI research worldwide.
That history matters for tonight's audience of open-hardware engineers. When Buck speaks about AI factory architecture, he is drawing on the same instinct that drove the creation of CUDA in 2007: that the constraint everyone accepts as fixed — in 2007, the GPU's inaccessibility to programmers; in 2026, the data center's geographic boundedness — is an engineering problem, not a physical law.
Buck holds a BS from Princeton as well as his Stanford doctorate, and has been central to NVIDIA's technical direction through the GPU computing era, the deep-learning era, and now the agentic AI era, as detailed in his Ian Buck official NVIDIA biography. His keynote will be the first major industry-facing presentation of all four architecture pillars together, with production data now behind at least one of them.
Spectrum-XGS: NVIDIA's Answer to the Geography Problem
The core claim NVIDIA will advance tonight is that Spectrum-XGS, first detailed at Hot Chips in August 2025, adds a "scale-across" capability to its Ethernet networking portfolio that did not previously exist. Where conventional data-center networking literature describes three tiers — scale-up (within a server), scale-out (across servers in one facility), and the WAN link between facilities — the NVIDIA Spectrum-XGS Hot Chips announcement proposes a Spectrum-XGS scale-across fourth layer that treats geographically separated clusters as a single logical fabric.
That claim changes the economics of where AI factories can be built. Until Spectrum-XGS, a single large training run had to live inside one facility: network latency and bandwidth constraints between sites made distributed training impractical at rack scale. If Spectrum-XGS delivers on its architectural promises, an operator will be able to spread a single training job across facilities in, say, Austin and Stockholm without the job experiencing those sites as separate. The practical result is that operators will no longer need to find a single campus capable of housing every GPU a frontier model requires — they will be able to build modularly, in locations chosen for power cost, land availability, or regulatory environment, and stitch them together through Spectrum-XGS fabric.
CoreWeave Oracle Spectrum-XGS deployment has already been announced, with both companies among the first operators named as Spectrum-XGS adopters.
How Does Spectrum-XGS Actually Work?
Three engineering mechanisms enable Spectrum-XGS's scale-across capability.
First, co-packaged optics switch technology: rather than using pluggable transceivers in standard form factors such as SFP or QSFP, co-packaged optics (CPO) integrates optical components directly into the switch package. The result is higher bandwidth density and lower power per bit than pluggable optics can achieve — critical when linking facilities across long-haul fiber, where every watt of transceiver overhead limits throughput.
Second, distance-aware congestion control algorithms: Spectrum-XGS carries intelligence about the latency profile of each link in the fabric and adjusts flow control in response to that profile. Standard congestion control algorithms assume uniform latency — a reasonable assumption inside one building, an incorrect one across cities. Spectrum-XGS treats heterogeneous latency as an input to the scheduler, not a failure mode to work around.
Third, Spectrum-XGS end-to-end fabric telemetry: the platform maintains a real-time view of the full fabric, from NIC to switch to optical link. This visibility is what allows the scale-across scheduler to treat geographically distributed GPU clusters as one system rather than two systems with a pipe between them.
Vera Rubin NVL72: The Rack That Already Has Production Numbers
NVIDIA announced the Vera Rubin NVL72 CES 2026 announcement at CES on January 5, 2026. The platform packs 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs into a single rack, connected by sixth-generation NVLink at 260 TB/s within the rack. The NVLink 6 rack-level bandwidth spec of 260 TB/s — the aggregate bandwidth within one rack — eliminates the interconnect as the bottleneck inside the rack so the GPUs can be fed at the rates their compute density demands. The Rubin GPU NVFP4 inference specs show each Rubin GPU delivering 50 petaFLOPS of NVFP4 inference throughput and 35 petaFLOPS of training throughput, backed by 288 GB of HBM4 memory per GPU at 22 TB/s memory bandwidth.
Those specifications became production numbers on September 30, 2026, when CoreWeave Vera Rubin production availability was announced, with Cognition — the company behind the Devin AI coding agent — as the first production customer. Cognition reported a Cognition 4.8x token throughput benchmark compared with the GB200 NVL72 it replaced. On DeepSeek R1 inference workloads, NVIDIA projects a 10x throughput per megawatt claim compared with prior-generation hardware — a figure that, if it holds at scale, changes the cost structure of inference providers materially.
The 260 TB/s intra-rack NVLink 6 bandwidth — versus the approximately 64 GB/s ceiling of PCIe 5.0 — is the architectural feature that makes the NVL72's GPU count practical: it eliminates the interconnect as the bottleneck inside the rack so the GPUs can be fed at the rates their compute density demands.
Vera CPU: Why NVIDIA Built Its Own Processor to Eliminate the Agentic AI Bottleneck
The Vera CPU custom Olympus core design inside the NVL72 is not a licensing agreement or a procurement choice — it is a ground-up NVIDIA design built around a specific observed problem in agentic AI workloads.
The problem: in agentic inference — where a model generates a chain of reasoning steps rather than a single output — roughly 75 percent of compute time is spent in the decode phase, during which the CPU can become a throughput bottleneck if its bandwidth to the GPU is insufficient. Standard x86 CPUs communicate with GPUs over PCIe 5.0, which maxes out at approximately 64 GB/s per x16 slot.
The Vera CPU, built on 88 custom Olympus cores, connects to Rubin GPUs via Vera CPU NVLink-C2C bandwidth spec at 1.8 TB/s — representing a 28x improvement in CPU-to-GPU bandwidth over PCIe 5.0 x16. Beyond bandwidth, Vera's multi-threading architecture assigns each thread full core bandwidth rather than sharing it across simultaneous threads the way conventional SMT designs do — meaning agents that launch parallel reasoning chains do not starve each other for memory bandwidth. In NVIDIA's benchmarks, the result is 1.8x faster agent task completion compared with x86-based configurations.
DSX: Software That Turns a Building Into an AI Factory Before the Hardware Arrives
NVIDIA made the NVIDIA DSX GTC Taipei announcement at GTC Taipei on May 31, 2026. DSX is a factory management stack with four components, each targeting a different operational constraint in the path from empty building to producing AI cluster.
DSX OS open-source operations software is an open-source platform for AI factory operations management, giving operators and OEMs a common instrumentation and orchestration layer. The DSX MaxLPS 45°C liquid cooling spec enables sustained 45°C coolant inlet temperatures, raising the GPU density achievable within a given power budget by approximately DSX MaxLPS 40 percent GPU density compared with traditional cooling approaches. That 40-percent improvement compounds: more GPUs per rack, less cooling overhead per GPU, and a facility design that can be sited in geographic locations where mechanical chilling would otherwise be prohibitively expensive. DSX Flex grid demand-response capability is a grid-responsive power management layer that allows an AI factory to participate in demand-response programs, potentially turning compute infrastructure into a grid asset rather than a pure load. DSX Sim AI factory digital twin is a digital twin tool that lets operators model an AI factory's thermal, power, and networking behavior before a single GPU is installed — reducing the risk of expensive post-build corrections.
The NVIDIA DSX OEM partner ecosystem of OEMs already shipping DSX-compatible hardware includes Dell, HPE, Lenovo, and Supermicro, alongside ASUS, Foxconn, GIGABYTE, Pegatron, QCT, Wistron, and Wiwynn. NVIDIA DSX cloud deployment partners include CoreWeave, Crusoe, Firmus, IREN, Lamb

articles.full_text:
In yet another surprising move for Call of Duty, Modern Warfare 4 studio Infinity Ward has announced that the game's extraction shooter mode, DMZ, will be released prior to the game's official launch. DMZ will be available starting 20th October for players who pre-order a copy digitally.
Modern Warfare 4 now effectively has three release dates. The campaign unlocks 16th October, DMZ four days later on the 20th, and the full launch - which is when multiplayer will be playable - arrives 23rd October.
Though Infinity Ward has offered campaign early access with other Modern Warfare titles in the past, doing the same for DMZ - a multiplayer mode - is certainly new. It's a potentially shrewd move, allowing DMZ to capture streamers and generate excitement about the game ahead of its release over an entire week, with a big blip every few days. It also allows players curious about DMZ to play it without feeling they ought to be making progress in multiplayer instead.
Seeing as DMZ has its own separate progression, however, players who jump in early could potentially have an advantage come launch if they manage to accrue many items, not to mention the map knowledge they would get from simply spending more time playing.
Separately, Infinity Ward hosted a Reddit Q&A focusing on DMZ, and the question of a PvE-only playlist came up. If you're unfamiliar, a recent first-look gameplay video showed an option for Single Squad Mission in DMZ, which players took to mean a mode free from other players. However, the option disappeared in a follow-up trailer, leading to confusion. So what's going on there? Infinity Ward has an explanation, albeit an unconvincing one.
"The playlist you saw is a developer playlist that was never intended to be for public use, it lets our team load into a match alone to work," the developer answered. "In the shipping game, players choose to be solo by turning off squad fill, but it's not guaranteed to be only solos in that lobby."
I'm not convinced. Though it's obviously possible for Single Squad to be a dev-only mode, they typically don't require bespoke icons. It's also curious that Infinity Ward didn't blur the image to cover that bit of it, which is commonly done in these sorts of behind-the-scenes videos of gameplay footage, whenever the camera captures something we're not supposed to see.
Modern Warfare 4 officially launches 23rd October on PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2.

articles.full_text:
Synopsis
Nvidia's share of China's market for data-centre AI chips fell to 34% in the first half of 2026, as US export controls restricted supplies of its products and domestic rivals led by Huawei gained ground, according to an IDC report seen by Reuters.
Washington has restricted China's access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips, limiting the range of products the US chipmaker can sell in the world's second-largest economy. Beijing, meanwhile, has promoted domestic alternatives and required Chinese companies to seek approval to import compliant Nvidia chips.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has repeatedly criticised Washington's export curbs, saying the policy forced a US company to cede China's $50 billion AI chip market to Huawei.
IDC did not specify which Nvidia products made up its 34% market share, or whether the figure included cutting-edge chips such as the B200 and B300, which are barred from export to China but have been smuggled into the country.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.
Huawei shipped 572,000 AI accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, giving it a 28% share of the overall market, IDC said.
Alibaba's chip-design unit T-Head held 7%, followed by Cambricon with 5%, Baidu's Kunlunxin with 4% and Hygon with 3%. Nine of the 11 Chinese chipmakers tracked by IDC increased shipments from a year earlier.
Total AI-accelerator shipments reached 2.008 million units in the first half. Shipments of graphics processing units, or GPUs - the chips most widely used to train AI models - fell 26% to 991,000 units, as supplies eligible for sale in mainland China remained limited, IDC said.
Shipments of other AI accelerators rose nearly 80% to 1.016 million units, overtaking GPUs by volume. This category includes chips designed for specific AI tasks, such as running trained models.
Huawei, T-Head, Kunlunxin and Cambricon together accounted for 95% of the non-GPU segment, which IDC said was being adopted by government agencies, internet companies and telecoms providers.
IDC said competition was shifting from the performance of a single chip to system-level capabilities, including how well chips work in a larger computing cluster.

articles.title: SpaceX launches Falcon 9 Starlink mission for 1st time in more than 3 weeks (photos) - Space
articles.summary: SpaceX launches Falcon 9 Starlink mission for 1st time in more than 3 weeks (photos)  Space
articles.full_text:
SpaceX just broke an uncharacteristically long Starlink launch drought.
The company sent 27 of its Starlink internet satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) today (Oct. 12), launching them atop a Falcon 9 rocket from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base at 8:28 p.m. EDT (5:28 p.m. local time; 0028 GMT on Oct. 13)
It was the first Starlink mission for a Falcon 9 since Sept. 19, which was another 27-satellite liftoff from Vandenberg. For some perspective on this recent gap: Between Aug. 19 and Sept. 6, a span of 19 days, SpaceX launched seven Starlink missions with Falcon 9s.
SpaceX did loft a batch of Starlinks after that, but it wasn't aboard a Falcon 9. The company's Starship megarocket carried 26 next-gen Starlink V3 craft on its 14th test flight, which took place on Sept. 28.
Starship reached orbit for the first time ever on Flight 14, and it deployed the Starlinks successfully as well. This will happen many more times going forward, if all goes to plan: The Starlink V3 constellation will eventually consist of about 100,000 satellites, all of which will fly on Starship, Elon Musk has said.
Indeed, SpaceX plans to sunset the Falcon 9 and its cousin, the Falcon Heavy, in the next few years, shifting their duties over to the fully reusable, far more powerful Starship, which remains in the test-flight phase.
That shift will be a big one for the spaceflight community, for the Falcon 9 is the workhorse rocket of its generation. In 2025, for example, it flew 165 times — roughly the same number as the rest of the world's orbital launchers combined. Nearly three-quarters of those Falcon 9 launches were Starlink missions.
Things have slowed down a bit in 2026. Today's flight was the 112th Falcon 9 liftoff of the year, and the 82nd in service of the Starlink megaconstellation, which currently consists of more than 11,100 active satellites.
All went according to plan on today's launch. The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth as planned, touching down about 8.5 minutes after launch on the drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed in the Pacific Ocean. It was the 20th launch and landing for this particular booster, which is designated B1088.
The rocket's expendable upper stage, meanwhile, delivered the 27 spacecraft to LEO, deploying them there 62 minutes after liftoff, SpaceX announced via X.

Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China from January through June, down 44 percent from a year earlier, IDC data showed. AI accelerators are specialised chips used to train and run AI models.
Washington has restricted China's access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips, limiting the range of products the US chipmaker can sell in the world's second-largest economy. Beijing, meanwhile, has promoted domestic alternatives and required Chinese companies to seek approval to import compliant Nvidia chips.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has repeatedly criticised Washington's export curbs, saying the policy forced a US company to cede China's US$50 billion (HK$390 billion) AI chip market to Huawei.
IDC did not specify which Nvidia products made up its 34 percent market share, or whether the figure included cutting-edge chips such as the B200 and B300, which are barred from export to China but have been smuggled into the country.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.
Huawei shipped 572,000 AI accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, giving it a 28 percent share of the overall market, IDC said.
Alibaba's (9988) chip-design unit T-Head held 7 percent, followed by Cambricon with 5 percent, Baidu's (9888) Kunlunxin with 4 percent and Hygon with 3 percent. Nine of the 11 Chinese chipmakers tracked by IDC increased shipments from a year earlier.
Total AI-accelerator shipments reached 2.008 million units in the first half. Shipments of graphics processing units, or GPUs — the chips most widely used to train AI models — fell 26 percent to 991,000 units, as supplies eligible for sale in mainland China remained limited, IDC said.
Shipments of other AI accelerators rose nearly 80 percent to 1.016 million units, overtaking GPUs by volume. This category includes chips designed for specific AI tasks, such as running trained models.
Huawei, T-Head, Kunlunxin and Cambricon together accounted for 95 percent of the non-GPU segment, which IDC said was being adopted by government agencies, internet companies and telecoms providers.
IDC said competition was shifting from the performance of a single chip to system-level capabilities, including how well chips work in a larger computing cluster.
IDC expects total accelerator shipments in China to grow 19 percent this year, even as GPU shipments fall 9 percent.

articles.summary: Zelensky Warns Chinese-Backed Rival to Starlink Will Soon Empower Russian Forces  Military Watch Magazine
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned that China could soon provide Russian forces with access to a satellite communications network comparable to SpaceX’s Starlink, potentially strengthening military communications and drone operations. The warning comes as Moscow accelerates development of its own low Earth orbit satellite internet constellation, known as Rassvet. Ukrainian sources have also argued that Chinese support could help bring the Russian system into service sooner and with more advanced capabilities than expected. “We are talking with various colleagues from Europe and America. I tell them honestly: Chinese representatives are involved in developing an alternative to Starlink,” Zelensky said. “They are getting closer, and they are passing it on to Russia. Russia could gain that kind of dominance.”
Zelensky has urged the United States to impose sanctions on Russian and Chinese firms involved in the programme, raising the issue with U.S. President Donald Trump during discussions that included a meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. According to reporting by the Financial Times, Zelensky is particularly concerned that the network could improve Russia’s ability to coordinate attacks using unmanned aerial vehicles. Rassvet currently remains far smaller than Starlink, which operates a constellation numbering in the thousands. Skibitskyi said the Russian system’s current capabilities over Ukraine were intermittent, with connectivity dependent on satellites passing overhead. Establishing a much larger constellation would permit more continuous coverage and could significantly improve the network’s usefulness for military communications.
Reliable satellite communications have become an important component of the war in Ukraine, supporting command networks, reconnaissance, logistics and the operation of unmanned systems. Starlink has been particularly valuable to Ukrainian forces because its low-orbit constellation can provide connectivity in areas where conventional communications infrastructure has been destroyed or disrupted. The network has also supported the operation of drones, allowing units to exchange information and maintain links over distances that would otherwise require more vulnerable communications infrastructure. A number of analysts have highlighted that the importance of Starlink for the Ukrainian war effort exceeds that of all support provided by European NATO members combined, as it prevented Russian forces from paralysing command and control in the war’s critical initial days.
Russian forces have notably also used Starlink terminals, including devices obtained through unofficial channels, despite restrictions imposed by SpaceX. Ukraine pressed the company to block unauthorised Russian military access, and the resulting disruption highlighted the risks of relying on a commercial communications network whose operator can restrict service. The United States has limited Ukraine’s access to Starlink for strikes deeper into Russian territory, and in February 2025 threatened wider cutoffs from the network. China’s defence sector is notably also developing means of countering Starlink, with laser weapons and attack satellites speculated to be among the methods considered.

articles.full_text:
Quantum computing is attracting fresh investment as technology companies accelerate development timelines and governments back the sector. The first fault-tolerant quantum computers could arrive around 2028 or 2029, according to expectations cited in The Daily Upside. But commercial adoption remains uncertain, leaving investors to decide how best to access the opportunity.
Two ETFs offer different approaches: the Defiance Quantum ETF QTUM and the WisdomTree Quantum Computing Fund (NYSE:WQTM).
QTUM- Broader Technology Exposure
QTUM tracks the BlueStar Machine Learning and Quantum Computing Index, which covers companies involved in quantum computing, machine learning, computing chips and related software. It held 90 stocks and has $5.74 billion in net assets, with an annual expense ratio of 0.40%.
Its portfolio extends beyond pure-play quantum developers. Global Unichip represents 2.33% of assets, which is currently the largest holding. Meanwhile Horizon Quantum Holdings Ltd HQ represents 1.87% and Palantir Technologies Inc PLTR represents 1.84%.
That breadth offers exposure to the wider computing ecosystem, but it also means QTUM’s performance can depend on machine learning, software and semiconductor trends rather than quantum breakthroughs alone.
QTUM returned 36% year to date, despite an 8% decline over the preceding three months. The contrast highlights the volatility investors may face even in a diversified portfolio.
Read Also: IonQ Stock Wins Analyst Backing Ahead of 2027 Superion Launch
WQTM Makes a More Direct Quantum Bet
WQTM allocates more of its portfolio to companies developing quantum technology. IonQ Inc IONQ represents 6.1% of assets, Quantinuum Inc QNT 5.6%, Rigetti Computing Inc RGTI 5.2% and D-Wave Quantum Inc QBTS 4.8%. IBM IBM, Microsoft Corp MSFT and Amazon.com, Inc AMZN provided exposure to larger technology businesses as well.
The fund had approximately $346 million in assets and charged a 0.45% annual expense ratio.
Its larger positions in quantum specialists could make it more responsive to technical breakthroughs and commercial contracts. However, those companies also face substantial uncertainty over error correction, scalability and the timing of revenue growth.
The Key Question Is Commercial Adoption
Quantum computers could eventually support drug discovery, materials science, financial modelling and supply-chain optimization. They are expected to complement conventional CPUs and GPUs, not simply replace them, according to The Daily Upside.
For investors, QTUM offers broader exposure to computing and machine learning, while WQTM tilts more heavily toward quantum developers. Neither guarantees gains if the technology takes longer than expected to become commercially useful.
The next test is whether progress in error correction and practical computing applications translates into repeatable customer demand and sustainable revenue. Until then, quantum ETFs remain a bet on an emerging technology rather than an established commercial market.

articles.title: China and the EU could turn Morocco into a surprise global hub for electric vehicles - The Conversation
articles.summary: China and the EU could turn Morocco into a surprise global hub for electric vehicles  The Conversation
articles.full_text:
China now makes more than seven in ten of the world’s electric cars. In 2024 it produced over 12 million, 1.25 million of which were exported, mainly to Europe.
The EU is worried about this – alarmed by cheap, state-subsidised Chinese vehicles flooding its market and threatening the 13 million jobs which depend on its own auto industry. So the bloc has spent the past two years building a system of tariffs and rules to keep Chinese cars at bay.
In 2024, it imposed extra duties of up to 35% on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs), on top of an existing 10% import tariff. So far though, the EU’s tactics have yielded limited results.
Chinese vehicle sales in Europe nearly doubled between 2024 and 2025.
And much of this sales volume is being driven by the EV powerhouse that is developing at speed in Morocco.
Chinese firms producing cars in Morocco avoid exposure to those EU tariffs, and have announced US$6 billion (£4.5 billion) of investment in battery and electric car component plants in the country.
As a production base, Morocco has plenty of other advantages too. Its deep-water port in Tangier is the largest in Africa and the Mediterranean. It is also surrounded by state-sponsored industrial zones built specifically for carmakers and their suppliers.
Like its neighbours, Morocco has a free trade agreement with the EU, but is the only north African country which has one with the US.
And crucially, it has a good supply of the critical minerals needed for making batteries for EVs, including around 70% of the world’s phosphate reserves and plenty of cobalt.
Nor is Morocco starting from scratch in the car manufacturing business. Cars are the country’s biggest export. Many Moroccan workers have been trained in automotive assembly thanks to two major car companies.
Renault and Stellantis (the owner of 14 car brands including Peugeot, Fiat and Alfa Romeo) form a manufacturing base in Morocco that exported US$17 billion in cars and parts in 2024. This made Morocco one of the EU’s largest automotive trading partners ahead of China.
Electric dreams
Of the 560,000 vehicles Morocco produced in 2024, the vast majority were petrol and diesel models. Only around 50,000 were electric.
But a new wave of investment can help the industry shift to green. Recent multi-billion-euro commitments from Stellantis and Renault will expand EV and hybrid capacity. At the same time, Chinese investment is filling domestic gaps in cathode and battery cell production.
This transformation did not happen to Morocco by chance. The government has spent two decades laying the groundwork.
It has built “free zones”, areas where businesses can import, manufacture, process and re-export goods without paying normal taxes or customs duties. These include automotive “clusters”, including the Tanger “automotive city”.
This year, Morocco introduced a carbon tax to keep its exports compliant with EU rules.
So Morocco has been positioning itself to benefit from the EU tariffs. Whether Morocco actually gains from this boom depends on what kind of production Chinese firms undertake.
They could treat Morocco as a mere transit hub, sending goods through Morocco with minimal processing purely to evade tariffs. Brussels has already caught one such case, ruling in 2025 that aluminium wheels shipped from Morocco were being unfairly subsidised by Beijing.
Or they could do the opposite: build real factories, share technology, train local engineers and buy from Moroccan suppliers. This is what would turn the current boom into lasting green industrialisation, of the type that the African Union wants to encourage, linking African mineral reserves to clean-energy manufacturing.
But there are potential stumbling blocks which could prevent Morocco from benefiting from this new wave of investment in the long term.
First, the EU rules themselves may not last. Its tariffs on Chinese electric cars are set for only five years, and legal challenges are already underway. Second, the technology may remain in Chinese hands. And third, the geopolitical and climate context is so volatile that business plans could change very quickly.
On the plus side, Morocco has an established manufacturing footprint and government support. So the unintended consequences of EU trade policy could end up producing one of the biggest green industrialisation stories of the next decade.
