articles.summary: Germany to invest €35B in military space defense and satellite constellations  Aerospace Global News
articles.full_text:
Russian military satellites that manoeuvred close to a Western surveillance spacecraft supporting Ukraine earlier this year have demonstrated capabilities that could threaten Elon Musk’s Starlink network and other commercial satellite constellations, Germany’s military space commander has warned.
Major General Michael Traut, speaking to Reuters on 9 October, said the Russian spacecraft had been “chasing” a satellite operated by Finnish company ICEYE, which provides radar imagery used for battlefield intelligence. He warned that similar operations against a large constellation such as Starlink could shorten the operational lives of satellites and disrupt services beyond Ukraine.
“Russia is demonstrating ways, which, if employed directly towards a mega constellation like Starlink, could have an impact on their lifetime” and on the quality of service for all users, not just Ukraine, General Traut told Reuters. He said satellite capabilities could be disrupted even without a direct attack. That “concerns me quite a lot,” he said.
The warning follows unusual orbital manoeuvres by four Russian military satellites, Cosmos 2610, 2611, 2612 and 2613, in May. Their movements towards ICEYE-X36 were first publicly identified in a 22 May analysis by Greg Gillinger, a former US Air Force space intelligence officer, who examined orbital tracking data and questioned Russia’s intentions.
ICEYE subsequently confirmed the incident to Reuters, while the US Space Force also documented the Russian activity.
The incident has added urgency to Western concerns about military operations in orbit, where spacecraft capable of approaching and following other satellites could interfere with communications and intelligence services without necessarily destroying their targets.
How four Russian satellites approached ICEYE
Gillinger, writing in an analysis published by US defence and intelligence consultancy Integrity ISR, identified substantial orbital changes involving four of six Russian Cosmos satellites launched in April.
Between 14-20 May, the four spacecraft increased their orbital inclination from approximately 97 degrees to 97.8 degrees, closely matching the orbital plane of ICEYE-X36, a synthetic aperture radar satellite operating about 547 kilometres above Earth.
Changing a satellite’s orbital inclination is an energy-intensive operation. Unlike a routine adjustment to maintain altitude, it requires a spacecraft to alter the angle of its orbital path.
Gillinger estimated that the Russian manoeuvres involved a velocity change of approximately 105 to 106 metres per second, representing a significant use of the satellites’ available propulsion capability.
The Russian spacecraft had already been launched into orbital planes relatively close to ICEYE-X36. Their subsequent adjustments brought them into nearly matching planes, with cross-track separations ranging from about 500 metres to 22 kilometres.
Those figures describe the distance between orbital paths, rather than necessarily the closest physical separation between the spacecraft.
The manoeuvres left the Russian satellites in positions from which further adjustments could bring them closer to ICEYE-X36, according to Gillinger’s assessment.
He cautioned that neither the spacecraft’s precise capabilities nor Russia’s intentions were known. The orbital changes nevertheless demonstrated an ability to carry out substantial manoeuvres that would be unusual for satellites performing conventional observation or communications missions.
ICEYE chief executive Rafal Modrzewski later told Reuters that the company moved its satellite, after which the Russian spacecraft made further orbital adjustments.
Belinda Marchand, chief scientist at US space intelligence company Slingshot Aerospace, told Reuters the activity could have been intended for surveillance, preparation for interference or a demonstration of capability.
There is no publicly established evidence that the Russian satellites attempted to damage ICEYE-X36.
Why the ICEYE satellite matters to Ukraine
ICEYE operates a constellation of synthetic aperture radar satellites capable of imaging the Earth’s surface in darkness and through cloud cover.
Unlike conventional optical satellites, which depend on sunlight and clear weather, radar spacecraft transmit signals towards the ground and measure their reflections.
The technology is particularly useful for monitoring military equipment, troop movements and infrastructure when poor weather or darkness would otherwise restrict surveillance.
ICEYE has provided imagery to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. An agreement announced that year gave the Ukrainian government access to a dedicated radar satellite and data from the company’s wider constellation.
Its role illustrates how private satellite operators have become increasingly important to military operations. Governments can obtain intelligence, surveillance and communications services from commercial constellations without having to develop and operate every spacecraft themselves.
Russia has previously warned that commercial space infrastructure used to support Ukraine could become a target.
In October 2022, Russian foreign ministry official Konstantin Vorontsov told a United Nations meeting that privately operated satellites supporting military operations could be considered legitimate targets.
Moscow has not disclosed the capabilities of the Cosmos spacecraft involved in the May manoeuvres. Russia’s defence ministry did not respond to Reuters’ questions about the incident.
Could Starlink face similar interference?
Starlink has become an important communications system for Ukrainian forces, particularly in areas where terrestrial networks have been damaged or destroyed.
Unlike a traditional satellite network built around a small number of large spacecraft, Starlink uses thousands of satellites in low Earth orbit. This makes the system more resilient to the loss of individual spacecraft, but it also creates a demanding task for operators trying to avoid collisions.
Traut told Reuters that Russia could use tactics falling short of a direct attack to interfere with such a network.
He described a hypothetical scenario in which a Russian spacecraft entered a Starlink orbital path and broke apart, creating debris that would force other satellites to manoeuvre away.
Such avoidance manoeuvres consume propellant, potentially shortening the satellites’ useful lives. A widespread disruption could also affect the quality of service provided to users.
An overt attack on Starlink would represent a major escalation, Traut said, but other forms of interference could be harder to classify or respond to.
His warning comes just days after SpaceX disclosed the scale of the collision-avoidance problem already confronting Starlink.
As AGN reported on 8 October, SpaceX said its satellites had encountered potential close-approach situations involving approximately 650 different manoeuvring spacecraft during 2026, with only about half providing trajectory information.
The company also reported approximately 164,000 potential collision events over six months, although most did not represent imminent collisions.
SpaceX highlighted an August encounter in which a Starlink satellite came within 134 metres of another spacecraft following an unexpected orbital change.
These were routine space-traffic safety concerns, not reported Russian attacks. They nevertheless show how difficult it can be to operate a large constellation when other spacecraft change their trajectories without providing advance information.
A deliberate attempt to force repeated avoidance manoeuvres would introduce another complication into an already crowded orbital environment.
SpaceX did not respond to Reuters’ request for comment on Traut’s warning.
Space warfare moves from surveillance to manoeuvring
The Russian activity comes as military powers increasingly prepare for operations in which satellites themselves could become targets.
For decades, spacecraft have provided communications, navigation, missile warning and intelligence to forces fighting on Earth. The growing concern is that an adversary could attack those capabilities directly in orbit.
The United States has been watching similar developments involving Chinese spacecraft.
As AGN reported in September, US military officials disclosed that Chinese satellites had conducted coordinated movements resembling orbital “dogfighting”. The term refers to spacecraft manoeuvring around one another to gain a favourable position, rather than the rapid turns associated with fighter aircraft.
China has also demonstrated technology capable of capturing a defunct satellite and moving it into another orbit. Such capabilities have legitimate applications in spacecraft servicing and debris removal, but they could also be used to interfere with another country’s satellites.
The US and its allies are developing their own ability to manoeuvre in orbit.
In September, US Space Command conducted Apollo Maneuvers 2026, its first live exercise involving coordinated spacecraft operations across low, medium and geosynchronous Earth orbits.
The exercise examined how satellites could move to avoid threats and continue operating in a contested environment. It also addressed the need for servicing and refuelling, since repeated orbital manoeuvres consume limited onboard propellant.
General Stephen Whiting, commander of US Space Command, explained the changing military requirement.
“Operating from a static, predictable orbit leaves our assets fighting from an easily targeted, fixed position,” he said.
The exercise followed a joint US-UK military satellite operation in September 2025, during which American forces directed a spacecraft towards a British satellite. Commercial tracking subsequently showed that a Chinese spacecraft had passed about 83 kilometres beneath the two allied satellites.

articles.title: Super Micro contractor pleaded guilty to smuggling $2.5B in Nvidia AI servers to China - Quartz
articles.summary: Super Micro contractor pleaded guilty to smuggling $2.5B in Nvidia AI servers to China  Quartz
articles.full_text:
Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun, a contractor linked to Super Micro Computer, pleaded guilty to four counts in connection with an illegal scheme to ship Nvidia $NVDA-powered AI servers to China, court records reveal, according to Reuters. Sun entered his plea in U.S. District Court in Manhattan on Thursday.
The charges cover four separate conspiracies: breaching U.S. export control laws, unlawfully removing goods from the country, defrauding the government, and obstructing justice. Sun is scheduled to be sentenced in September 2027, according to The Next Web.
Prosecutors charged Sun and two others in March with conspiring to divert roughly $2.5 billion worth of U.S. AI technology to China in violation of export laws. The operation started around October 2023, when Sun and his co-conspirators allegedly began shipping servers made by a U.S. company — widely understood to be Super Micro — into China without obtaining the licenses required under export law. Court documents portray Sun as a broker and "fixer" who arranged transactions and worked to keep the operation hidden from authorities.
Sun also arranged for fake "dummy" servers to be placed on-site in December 2025 and lied to a U.S. Department of Commerce official who came to inspect units that had in fact already been shipped to China, according to the indictment. According to authorities, he and his co-conspirators funneled Nvidia-powered servers through a Southeast Asian intermediary, which ultimately delivered them to end customers in China. The indictment named Nvidia's B200, H100, and H200 graphics processing units, and servers containing them, as subject to U.S. export restrictions.
March's charges also named Super Micro co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw and Ruei-Tsang "Steven" Chang, a sales manager based at Super Micro's Taiwan office. Liaw co-founded Super Micro in 1993 and joined its board in 2023. According to The Next Web, Liaw has pleaded not guilty and has left the company's board. Chang has not appeared in court.
Super Micro is not named as a defendant. The California-based company said the case has no impact on its business operations and that it terminated Sun and cut ties with the other defendants earlier this year. Super Micro said in August that its current senior leaders had no knowledge of the scheme and that it is cooperating with investigators.
The case is part of a broader effort by U.S. authorities to enforce restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China. Washington has barred Nvidia's advanced AI chips from reaching China since 2022, citing national security concerns. The U.S. and China are competing for dominance in AI, with both investing heavily in technology seen as critical to economic growth and military capabilities.
Taiwan prosecutors separately charged nine people — including former employees of Nvidia and Super Micro — with facilitating the shipment of dozens of advanced AI servers to China in violation of U.S. export controls. Prosecutors in Taiwan have said it is too early to determine whether the two investigations are connected.

articles.title: Explained: Why Starlink's India launch plans have raised security concerns - Business Standard
articles.summary: Explained: Why Starlink's India launch plans have raised security concerns  Business Standard
articles.full_text:
Elon Musk-backed Starlink is yet to launch its satellite internet services in India, despite securing a Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite (GMPCS) licence and authorisation from the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe). The company is awaiting security clearances and spectrum assignment amid concerns over the risks of placing a foreign-controlled network. 
This comes amid Musk’s allegations on X that Indian “oligarchs” were delaying Starlink’s entry to protect their “monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people”, targeting domestic telecom giants such as 
Mukesh Ambani
’s Reliance Jio. The Ministry of Communications and Union Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia rejected the allegations as “baseless and misconceived”, asserting that India’s satellite communications framework was fair and non-discriminatory.
What are the key security risks associated with Starlink?
A report by the Takshashila Institution, titled 'Starlink and Risks for India,' flags concerns over government control of connectivity, potential misuse of user data, foreign influence and the difficulty of blocking unauthorised terminals.
 
The report warns that Starlink’s dependence on a foreign private operator could limit the government’s control over connectivity during a national security crisis. Services could remain active when authorities want them suspended or be switched off when connectivity is needed.
Ukraine illustrates this risk. After Starlink began operating there in February 2022, the country became heavily dependent on the service for government and military communications. Musk reportedly restricted access multiple times through geofencing and denied the Ukrainian military’s request to activate the service, affecting operations. The report warns that similar restrictions could disrupt communications in India’s sensitive border regions.
 
National security risks from unauthorised terminals
Beyond the risk of service disruption, the report warns that Starlink could potentially use sensitive user data for intelligence purposes or commercial gain. In India, security agencies have seized unauthorised Starlink hardware in incidents linked to narcotics trafficking and regional insurgencies.
In the Andaman Sea and off Gujarat, security forces intercepted foreign vessels carrying large narcotics consignments and recovered Starlink Mini terminals. Along the Punjab border, intelligence agencies seized Starlink hardware linked to cross-border drug syndicates involved in drone-based smuggling operations. In Manipur, security forces recovered a Starlink satellite antenna and router during a raid amid ethnic violence. The recovery raised concerns that insurgent groups could use smuggled satellite internet to bypass state-imposed internet shutdowns.
 
Geopolitical leverage and foreign influence
The report also raises concerns about the geopolitical implications of relying on a network controlled by a foreign company. It argues that Musk could use his influence in Washington to advance Starlink’s commercial interests, potentially exposing India to diplomatic pressure if its regulations conflict with the company’s plans.
Musk played a prominent role in Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign and later became the de facto head of the Department of Government Efficiency. Despite their public falling-out in 2025, the two have maintained a political relationship. SpaceX also launches satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office and the US Space Force, supports missile warning and tracking, and undertakes human spaceflight and Artemis missions for Nasa.
 
The report notes that SpaceX’s reliance on US government contracts, regulatory approvals, spectrum allocations and orbital licences could give Washington leverage over the company. If US and Indian interests diverged, Washington could potentially pressure SpaceX to share data collected in India, maintain connectivity in certain regions or restrict services elsewhere.
Data privacy concerns
Apart from the geopolitical risks, the report flags concerns over Starlink’s data-handling practices. On January 15, 2026, the company updated its Global Privacy Policy to permit customer data, including location information, IP addresses and communication information such as audio, electronic or visual information, to be used to train artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning models.
 
The policy also permits sharing this data with unnamed third-party collaborators for AI training, with users opted in by default. The report raises concerns that these provisions could create potential avenues for surveillance and data misuse.
Why is blocking unauthorised Starlink use difficult?
The report points to the technical challenges of controlling satellite internet access. Starlink satellites orbit about 60 times closer to Earth than geostationary satellites, giving each satellite a smaller footprint. This makes Low Earth Orbit (LEO) constellations inherently more difficult to block than traditional geostationary Earth Orbit (GEO) systems.
What lessons do Ukraine and Iran offer?
The report highlights the risks of relying on a foreign private operator during a national crisis. Since 2022, Russia has reportedly used GPS jamming to disrupt Ukraine’s Starlink connectivity, highlighting the vulnerability of satellite internet to electronic interference.
 
Iran faced similar challenges. An estimated 50,000 smuggled Starlink terminals were operating illegally there at the beginning of 2026. When authorities shut down terrestrial internet amid protests in January, Starlink became a key link to the outside world.
Iran responded with GPS and radio-frequency jamming, drone surveillance and raids to seize terminals, causing localised and temporary disruptions. The country also complained to the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) over alleged violations of its sovereignty.
What security requirements has India set?
In May 2025, the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) issued security requirements for Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite (GMPCS) service providers, supplementing existing licence conditions. Operators, including Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Reliance Jio Satellite Communications, must obtain applicable security clearances before commencing commercial services.
 
Among the key requirements are provisions governing the routing of Indian traffic, the domestic location of network infrastructure, lawful interception and the monitoring of user terminals.
All Indian user traffic must pass through gateways located in India. Operators cannot bypass these gateways through inter-satellite links or mirror Indian traffic to overseas systems. Network control and monitoring centres, data centres and Points of Presence must also be located domestically, while Domain Name System (DNS) resolution must take place within the country.
Operators must comply with lawful interception and monitoring requirements and facilitate prescribed metadata collection by the DoT’s Telecom Security Operations Centre (TSOC). They must also share user-terminal location information with authorised agencies, enforce geofencing and comply with directions to restrict or suspend services in specified areas or for designated users. For land-based mobile terminals, location reporting is required every 2.6 km of movement or every minute, whichever occurs first.
 
The requirements also mandate support for monitoring in designated border and coastal areas, measures to prevent terminals from spoofing their locations, and controls to stop unauthorised terminals from circumventing domestic restrictions. Operators must also block websites prohibited by Indian authorities.
How has Starlink responded to security concerns?
While India’s requirements seek to establish greater oversight of satellite internet services, Starlink has argued that its entry would expand consumer choice, foster competition and help lower prices.
Musk has accused Indian business groups, including Reliance Jio, of using their influence to protect established market positions and delay the company’s launch. He has alleged that commercial interests, rather than security concerns, are driving the regulatory hurdles. Starlink maintains that it has been adapting its operations and data protocols to meet India’s licensing and regulatory requirements.

articles.title: Intel, Broadcom CEOs warn capital crunch could become AI's biggest bottleneck - CNBC
articles.summary: Intel, Broadcom CEOs warn capital crunch could become AI's biggest bottleneck  CNBC
articles.full_text:
SINGAPORE — The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom warned that access to capital could emerge as a major constraint on the artificial intelligence boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply.
Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said financing could become a bigger obstacle to AI expansion than shortages of semiconductors, memory chips or electricity, as the industry races to build the infrastructure needed to power increasingly sophisticated models.
″[What] I think might be the biggest constraint is capital,” Hock Tan said at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday.
Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan echoed concerns about financing, pointing to the rising cost of capital and questions over whether companies investing heavily in AI will eventually generate sufficient returns.
“If there’s any challenge in the front, it’s capital and the cost of capital, and then the other part is in the longer run, people want to see the ROI,” he said.
Their remarks highlight an emerging challenge for the AI industry, which has poured enormous sums into data centers, advanced chips and power infrastructure in anticipation of surging demand for computing capacity.
The warnings come as rising borrowing costs threaten to complicate financing for technology companies investing heavily in AI infrastructure. Higher bond yields could make it more expensive to fund data center construction and chip purchases, potentially putting pressure on the economics of projects that may take years to generate returns.
Hock Tan said the industry has repeatedly encountered supply bottlenecks over the past two years, but expects some of those constraints to ease as production capacity expands.
″[In the] last two years we have seen a series of bottlenecks that keep coming out, but then we overcome it,” he said. “Memory shortage today might not be that way a year from now.”
He suggested that wafer shortages could ease by 2028 or 2029, while power availability could also improve as new infrastructure comes online.
Despite the financing concerns, both executives remained bullish on near-term demand for AI computing infrastructure.
“There is more demand for compute infrastructure than we can supply,” Hock Tan said, adding that the imbalance could persist through 2029 and potentially into 2030.
Intel’s Tan similarly said the industry was unlikely to experience a significant slowdown over the next two to three years, citing growing adoption of AI applications and demand for computing power.
But sustaining that growth beyond the next few years will depend on how quickly businesses adopt AI and whether the technology delivers meaningful economic benefits, the executives said.
Broadcom’s Tan cautioned that demand for computing infrastructure could slow if the adoption of advanced AI models disappoints or improvements in their capabilities begin to plateau.
Lip-Bu Tan, meanwhile, emphasized that companies would increasingly need to demonstrate tangible returns from AI investments through improved efficiency and new business models.

articles.title: Largest EV Manufacturers in 2026: BYD vs Tesla, Geely and Volkswagen - GreentechLead
articles.summary: Largest EV Manufacturers in 2026: BYD vs Tesla, Geely and Volkswagen  GreentechLead
articles.full_text:
BYD leads Tesla in electric car sales through September 2026, while Geely and Volkswagen are strengthening their positions through expanding model ranges and regional growth.
The race among the world’s largest electric vehicle manufacturers is becoming more competitive. Sales volumes matter, but battery costs, affordable models, overseas expansion and profitability determine which companies can sustain growth.
Among BYD, Tesla, Geely Automobile and Volkswagen Group, BYD recorded the highest battery electric vehicle sales in 2025. Its lead continued during the first nine months of 2026, although the companies’ results reveal different strengths and challenges.
EV Sales Comparison: Why Vehicle Categories Matter
Electric vehicle comparisons require consistent definitions. Battery electric vehicles (BEVs) run entirely on electricity, while plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) combine rechargeable batteries with combustion engines.
BYD and Geely sell both categories. Tesla sells battery electric vehicles exclusively. Comparing BYD’s combined plug-in sales with Tesla’s deliveries would therefore overstate BYD’s advantage in the fully electric market.
The following table compares reported BEV sales for four major manufacturers. It is a selected comparison rather than a complete global ranking.
| Manufacturer | Reported BEV sales in 2025 | Reporting scope | 
| BYD | 2,256,714 | Passenger battery electric vehicles | 
| Tesla | 1,636,129 | Global vehicle deliveries | 
| Geely Automobile | 1,073,805 | Geely Automobile’s reported brands | 
| Volkswagen Group | 983,100 | Group battery electric vehicles, including commercial vehicles | 
The figures show that Geely Automobile exceeded one million BEV sales and finished ahead of Volkswagen Group in this comparison. Differences in reporting scope still matter when assessing market position.
BYD vs Tesla in 2026: Who Is Selling More Electric Cars?
BYD sold 1,629,957 passenger BEVs between January and September 2026, according to its September 2026 sales disclosure. Tesla delivered 1,324,681 vehicles over the same period, based on its three quarterly announcements.
That puts BYD ahead by approximately 305,000 vehicles, or 23 percent relative to Tesla’s deliveries. These are year-to-date results, so they do not establish the final 2026 outcome. www1.hkexnews.hk
BYD’s results also demonstrate why the BEV–PHEV distinction matters. Its passenger BEV sales increased 1.5 percent year on year through September, while PHEV sales fell 10.2 percent. Total new energy vehicle sales, including commercial vehicles, declined approximately 3.9 percent. Growth in fully electric cars therefore coexisted with weaker overall plug-in sales. www1.hkexnews.hk
For manufacturers, a broad product range provides access to different buyers. Compact electric cars target price-sensitive customers, while plug-in hybrids appeal to drivers seeking electric commuting with combustion-engine flexibility.
Tesla: High Volumes From a Concentrated Product Range
Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter of 2026, according to its Q3 production and delivery report.
Model 3 and Model Y accounted for 478,237 deliveries, approximately 98.3 percent of the quarterly total. Other models contributed 8,295 vehicles.
This concentration supports large production runs, but it makes performance heavily dependent on two core models. Pricing, product updates and competition in the electric sedan and SUV segments consequently have a substantial influence on Tesla’s sales.
Tesla retains a strong position at the individual-model level. The IEA estimates that Model Y represented nearly 8 percent of global BEV sales in 2025, while Model 3 accounted for approximately 3.6 percent.
Geely: Rapid EV Growth Across Multiple Brands
Geely Automobile’s BEV sales increased 86 percent to 1,073,805 vehicles in 2025. It also sold 613,962 plug-in hybrids, taking combined plug-in sales to approximately 1.69 million, according to Geely Automobile’s 2025 sales announcement.
Its reported portfolio includes Geely, Zeekr and Lynk & Co. These figures should not be confused with the entire Zhejiang Geely Holding portfolio, which includes additional automotive businesses.
The brand mix creates several routes to growth. Geely addresses mainstream demand, Zeekr competes in premium electric vehicles, and Lynk & Co expands the group’s electrified offering.
Financial performance adds another perspective. Geely Automobile reported RMB173.6 billion in first-half 2026 revenue, up 15 percent, and a 17.9 percent gross margin. These are company-wide figures covering its business, rather than standalone EV profitability measures.
Volkswagen: European Growth Offsets Weakness in China
Volkswagen Group delivered 983,100 BEVs in 2025, an increase of approximately 32 percent. Fully electric vehicles represented 10.9 percent of its total deliveries, according to its Volkswagen Group’s 2025 global delivery results.
Regional performance varied sharply:
Europe: 742,800 BEVs, up 65.9 percent.
China: 115,500 BEVs, down 44.3 percent.
United States: 72,000 BEVs, up 45.7 percent.
Within the group, Škoda delivered 174,900 BEVs, increasing 119.8 percent, while Audi delivered 223,000, up 35.6 percent. These examples show how growth across several brands can support group performance even when one major market weakens.
Volkswagen’s challenge is to convert growing electric vehicle demand into consistent performance across regions, where prices, competitors and customer preferences differ.
Affordable Models Are Reshaping EV Competition
The market extends beyond these four manufacturers. Smaller, affordable vehicles are gaining significant volumes alongside premium SUVs.
The IEA estimates that Geely’s Geome Xingyuan accounted for 3.5 percent of worldwide BEV sales in 2025, followed by the Wuling Hongguang Mini EV at 3.1 percent and BYD Seagull at 3 percent.
These examples demonstrate that manufacturers can build scale by meeting everyday transport needs. Purchase price, practical range and access to charging can be more influential than maximum battery capacity.
Battery Costs and Profitability Will Shape the Winners
Battery economics remains central to EV competitiveness. BloombergNEF reported that average lithium-ion battery pack prices fell 8 percent to $108 per kilowatt-hour in 2025. Its average for BEV packs was $99 per kilowatt-hour.
Consider an illustrative 60 kWh battery: a $10-per-kWh cost reduction would save $600 per vehicle. Across one million vehicles, that equals $600 million before other manufacturing costs and commercial factors.
However, higher sales do not automatically produce higher profits. Discounts, factory utilisation, warranty expenses and overseas expansion costs can absorb production savings.
Who Leads the Global EV Market in 2026?
BYD leads these manufacturers in reported BEV volume through September 2026. Tesla remains highly competitive through its core models, Geely has demonstrated rapid expansion, and Volkswagen has achieved strong European growth.
The decisive measures are profitable sales, competitive battery costs and sustained customer demand. Manufacturers that combine those advantages with affordable products will be better positioned to turn EV adoption into lasting business growth. 
SHAFANA FAZAL

articles.full_text:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind



The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp.



A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining.



That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will.



Find out what stands in the way of a city on the moon.



—Robin George Andrews



This story is from the next issue of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get your hands on a copy as soon as it lands on Wednesday 21 October!  



10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Brimstone and its one-stop process for making cleaner cement and critical minerals



Brimstone is one of MIT Technology Review’s10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.



Brimstone is a code-switching climate tech company for these polarized political times. The US startup is part green cement company, part critical mineral producer.



During the Biden administration, its primary pitch was cement that generates about 60% fewer greenhouse-gas emissions. It achieves this by switching to silicate rocks instead of standard limestone, which releases carbon dioxide when heated.



Under the Trump administration, however, the company is emphasizing another benefit of its process: the ability to extract valuable materials from those same rocks.



Discover how it’s making strides on two industrial problems.



—James Temple



Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch, spanning everything from geothermal power plants to smart turbines and semi-solid-state cells.



Job titles of the future: Delivery drone air traffic controller



The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,” he says. “I just immediately wanted to be a part of it.”



Wischnewsky is now an RPIC, or remote pilot in command, at a company called FlyTrex. An RPIC is like an air traffic controller. But instead of airplanes, they oversee fleets of drones that ferry cargo to homes and businesses



Here’s what it takes to become a drone air traffic controller.



—Eamon Whalen



The must-reads



I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.



1 An Anthropic AI model submitted a fake tip about an unsolved murderThe tip was in a new group of rogue actions Anthropic disclosed. (NYT $)+ Police criticised the company for waiting nine days to report it after finding it. (WSJ $)+ Another model submitted real government forms. (Quartz)+ The White House has made AI incident reporting mandatory. (Axios)+ But who’s liable when AI agents go rogue? (MIT Technology Review)



2 Ukraine’s drone strikes have dealt a major blow to Russian AISunday’s attack shut down the third Yandex data centre hit in days. (Reuters $)+ The strikes have disrupted Russia’s AI, cloud services, and apps. (Gizmodo)+ They followed Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers. (Ars Technica)+ Russian military satellites could disrupt Starlink. (Reuters $)+ Ukraine’s drone data is fueling a wild market. (MIT Technology Review)



3 Iranian ChatGPT users have planted AI-generated articles in news outletsAbout a dozen outlets ran roughly 100 articles by fake journalists. (CNN)+ The articles criticised the Iran war’s effects on Americans. (WP $)+ AI has been used to turn the Iran conflict into theatre. (MIT Technology Review)



4 Tesla has renamed “Full Self-Driving” as “Assisted Driving” in EuropeEU lawmakers said the old name was misleading.  (TechCrunch)+ Tesla hopes the rebrand leads regulators to approve the feature. (Wired $)+ Back in the US, it plans to increase toxic emissions near a school. (SFGate)



5 A ransomware negotiator has been arrested amid a hacking crackdownThe FBI suspects he was involved with a gang that recently claimed to have stolen data on the bureau’s employees. (Reuters $)+ AI is making online crimes easier. (MIT Technology Review)



6 Hollywood’s hottest villain right now is the tech billionaireFour new films feature dark depictions of Silicon Valley leaders. (Axios $)+ The real Mark Zuckerberg has also become a new character. (NYT $)



7 A new experiment is testing the Amazon’s response to rising CO₂CO₂-releasing towers will simulate future atmospheric conditions. (Nature)+ Is carbon removal in trouble? (MIT Technology Review)



8 The US hybrid boom has pushed some used car prices above new onesBuyers are paying a premium to skip the wait for new models. (Wired $)



9 A new technology switches tattoos on and off with lightIt can make permanent ink invisible. (New Scientist $)



10 Scientists spotted the most distant signal yet from the ancient universeIt could help them understand how the universe has evolved. (404 Media)



Quote of the day



“Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI.” 



—Microsoft’s president, Brad Smith, tells the BBC why AI urgently needs more regulations, including requiring firms to write “incident reports” and tell victims if the technology goes rogue.



One more thing



LINDA NYLIND / EYEVINE VIA REDUX




Geoffrey Hinton tells us why he’s now scared of the tech he helped build



Geoffrey Hinton is a pioneer of deep learning who helped develop some of the most important techniques at the heart of modern artificial intelligence, but after a decade at Google, he’s stepped down to focus on concerns he now has about AI.



Hinton is now spending his time on what he describes as “more philosophical work.” And that will focus on the small but—to him—very real danger that AI will turn out to be a disaster. Here’s why he’s so worried.



—Will Douglas Heaven



We can still have nice things

articles.title: Beyond the solvent fog: watching molecules dance in the crowd
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02970-yA technique called time-resolved X-ray liquidography has been used to shed precision light on the steps involved in a classic chemical reaction.
articles.full_text:
- NEWS AND VIEWS
Beyond the solvent fog: watching molecules dance in the crowd
One of the greatest challenges in modern physical chemistry — monitoring how molecules behave, interact and transform in a crowded liquid environment — seems simple, yet is anything but. Writing in Nature, Kim et al.1 apply the technique of time-resolved X-ray liquidography to the study of a textbook chemical reaction — the light-induced rearrangement of atoms in azobenzene molecules in solution. In doing so, the authors reveal details of this photoisomerization process and demonstrate the technique’s utility for studying low-mass atoms in a bulky solvent.

The woman died on Saturday, October 10. The advisory noted that the woman's death meets the definition of a measles death set by the state's health department.

articles.title: [不同来源] Epic Games reportedly pivoting to "AI first" game development model
articles.summary: "No more hand-written code" or AI-free art for delayed Marvel/Star Wars shooter.
articles.full_text:
Epic Games is shifting to an "AI first" development strategy for its collaboration with the Walt Disney Company, letting AI models write all the code and guide all the artwork for an upcoming shooter. That's according to a Bloomberg report, which cites unnamed people familiar with the project who commented on the significant pivot in internal development at the Unreal Engine maker.
Human developers will be tasked with managing and guiding code and art assets generated by models such as Anthropic's Claude, according to internal Epic employee messages viewed by Bloomberg. That means "no more hand-written code" and art assets "generated with full AI workflows," according to the report.
The $1.5 billion collaboration between Epic and Disney, announced in early 2024, was slated to release a Marvel- and Star Wars-themed shooter in March 2027. That project has now been delayed indefinitely amid the AI-related shakeup and understaffed, slower-than-expected development thus far, according to the report.Read full article

articles.summary: Kojima's discontinued "playable trailer" is no longer stuck on a few aging PS4 hard drives.
articles.full_text:
For over a decade now, the only "official" way to play Hideo Kojima's cult classic, P.T.—the long-discontinued "playable trailer" for Kojima's canceled "Silent Hills" project—has been via one of the increasingly rare PlayStation 4s that previously downloaded a copy during its monthslong availability window. Now, though, one coder is helping to preserve the game with a porting tool that builds a playable x86 PC executable from the original PS4 files.
Coder Lorean Xavier said he was inspired to work on the "P.T. for PC" project "because P.T. deserved to keep existing somewhere other than on consoles that still have it installed." The open source porting effort rebuilds the P.T. engine in C++ and Vulkan, using the original files from the PS4 game to re-create "every level, model, texture, sound, script and cutscene," according to its GitHub listing. That means players without their own legitimate decrypted copy of the original P.T. will have to track one down in order to generate a playable PC version.
The reliance on real P.T. files makes this port more authentic than previous hobbyist efforts to re-create the look and feel of P.T. for a PC audience. And while PS4 emulators recently reached a point where they could run P.T. completely, this native port also sports extra features, like upscaling and frame-generation, a camera mode, experimental third-person and VR support, and a "museum" section where you can look at and listen to in-game assets (including "unused content").Read full article

articles.title: F1 in Singapore: There's a new fastest car now
articles.summary: Also, F1’s final sprint saw our first real wet racing of the year.
articles.full_text:
Formula 1’s lengthy 2026 season is entering its final stretch. The sport took to the floodlit streets of Singapore on Sunday night, but Saturday saw action, too; this Grand Prix weekend was also the final of six sprints this year. The night race might be one of modern F1’s greatest spectacles. From overhead shots, the track becomes a bright, illuminated ribbon among the looming darkness of the city-state’s overpasses and skyscrapers. At ground level, the cars shower glittering sparks from their titanium skid blocks as the drivers flirt with how close they can get to the walls. As tracks go, the 90-degree turns and concrete barrier-lined streets were a world away from the abrasive tarmac and ample runoff of Malaysia last time out. But the tropical heat and humidity were a constant given both locations’ proximity to the equator.
Showers for the sprint
In Malaysia (which was still technically the Bahrain GP), a pre-race downpour disrupted things mightily. On Saturday morning in Singapore, shortly before the start of the sprint, it seemed history was about to rhyme when the skies opened. With standing water in places on the track, the sprint was delayed by 30 minutes. The sprint format, where a short extra race replaces a practice session a day before the main event, is unloved by the drivers and teams. For one thing, there’s little prestige in winning Saturday’s sprint. And with qualifying just a few hours later, risk-taking is discouraged lest one wreck the car and ruin Sunday’s race a day early.

      Oh no, not again!
        Credit:
          Mark Thompson/Getty Images
      
And in Singapore, like most street circuits, the proximity of the unyielding barriers that line the track means there are real, punishing consequences for getting it even a little wrong.Read full article

articles.full_text:
No organization in the world operates more robots than Amazon. The company already has more than 1 million robots working in warehouses around the clock to make tens of millions of same-day and one-day package deliveries happen on a daily basis—and Amazon is poised to significantly grow that robotic fleet in the coming years as it establishes new factories to churn out increasingly more capable robot workers.
Despite deploying so many robots, Amazon is also the second-largest corporate employer in the world, with more than 1.5 million full-time and part-time human workers, according to its 2025 annual report. Amazon executives say that the growing robot fleet has eased the burden on its human workforce by taking on the toughest fulfillment center tasks that carry the greatest risks of physical fatigue and injury. But labor advocacy groups and independent researchers point to evidence suggesting that warehouse automation driven by AI is not all upside for the humans who work alongside robots.
“For the last 100 years, most of the automation that we've seen usually happens away from workers—you're taking that high-risk task away from the worker, and you're doing so in a way that is not physically proximate,” Brian Greenwood, professor of business at George Mason University, told Ars. “The rise of collaborative robots really changes that dynamic for two reasons: one is that it is physically proximate, and two, the robot has the ability to dictate the pace of work.”Read full article

articles.title: Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind
articles.summary: Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a…
articles.full_text:
Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies. And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp. There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars.



The notion of a moon base, fanciful as it might sound, isn’t new. But this year, under the leadership of Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA has been flooding the zone with bold announcements. If all goes according to plan—a plan that will likely cost tens of billions of dollars to start—there will be drones, robotic landers, communication satellites, and a nuclear power plant; there will be plant terrariums and moonquake sensors; there will be mechanized scouts exploring craters for water.





Initial astronaut missions to the lunar surface, which the US is currently planning to start in 2028, will be focused on exploration and technological experimentation. But the idea is that we will—some time in the 2030s—get to a point where there will be habitation quarters for long-term stays, surrounded by a network of scientific research stations, resource mining and processing plants, and landing pads for spaceships. “It’s going to be an expanse,” says Carlos García-Galán, NASA’s moon base program manager—one that will add up to “hundreds of square miles.”



The effort is undoubtedly being fueled by nationalistic competition. China has near-identical plans to build its own base on the moon. And being first matters, because the “victor” gets to define the terms. What is the moon, exactly? Is it a militarized outpost? Is it a manufacturing hub? Is it a wilderness to be studied and preserved?



But there are also other reasons to go. Earth’s companion contains primeval rocks that hold clues to the formation of the entire solar system. The lunar surface, with virtually no atmosphere in the way, is an ideal place to put telescopes that could examine the most ancient epochs of the cosmos. The far side of the moon would be “a fantastic place to explore the further universe,” says Josef Aschbacher, the European Space Agency’s director general. And it’s way more energy efficient to launch rockets from the low-gravity lunar surface than it is from Earth, meaning sending astronauts—or robotic spacecraft—farther into the solar system will become much less difficult. “The moon is critical. It will be a stepping stone for going further—that means to Mars and beyond,” says Aschbacher.



SELMAN DESIGN




But if these bold visions are to become reality, there’s a daunting amount of work to be done. A sprawling moon base must be safe for its astronaut inhabitants—protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining, so that it can weather changing political fortunes and not cost ruinous amounts of money to maintain. For that, we’ll need to find a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating—and ideally generating revenue. And we’ll need autonomous robots that can build, maintain, and expand the base even when their human masters aren’t present. “It’s almost like starting civilization from scratch,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales.



Assuming we can overcome these starting challenges, decades from now—let’s say, by the year 2100—our initial moon bases could grow from barely visible structures into luminous cities, perhaps not too dissimilar from those dreamed up by authors and screenwriters the world over. “It’s like science fiction today that we really want to turn into a reality,” says García-Galán. Will anyone succeed?







The moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. In general, daytime temperatures can reach more than 250 °F; at night, they can plummet to less than –200 °F. Exposed to the vacuum of space, the surface is constantly showered in carcinogenic radiation and frequently hit by meteoroids. And its volcanic dust is sticky and corrosive, a destroyer of equipment and choker of lungs. 



Sadly, the lunar south pole—the area NASA is targeting—is even harsher. NASA wants to build a base there because its permanently shadowed craters are thought to harbor caches of water ice, which would be more precious than gold. Purify it, and you can water crops and hydrate astronauts; split it into oxygen and hydrogen, and you have breathable air and rocket propellant. But the temperature in those craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe. On the surface outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night.



But there is only so much money we can spend on safety. “What it comes down to is acceptable risk of death,” Philip Metzger, a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute, said while pondering some of the dangers. “What can we reasonably survive without breaking the bank?”



Temperature is one of the easiest problems to handle. Materials science has come a long way, and there are myriad metals, ceramics, plastics, compounds, and alloys that can resist wild temperature swings. Radiators keep things cool; heaters keep batteries from dying prematurely. Astronauts survive just fine too, with their fancy spacesuits—but that technology has proved itself only during brief excursions. It’s not yet clear how long this equipment could operate under such tempestuous conditions.

Outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night.




Space radiation, which can wreak havoc on electronics and trigger a cancerous division of cells, is far more pernicious. And as Stuart George, a physicist at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, explains, it comes in two unpleasant forms. 



The first is galactic cosmic rays, which rain down on the moon almost constantly. “They’re made by supernovas and neutron star mergers—all these kinds of things,” says George. And because the atomic nuclei, protons, and electrons that make them up are moving at significant fractions of the speed of light, these cosmic rays have oodles of kinetic energy, meaning they can punch through thin shielding (say, a metal wall) with ease. “They also have this habit where the heavier ions are fragmenting in that shielding and making secondary particles,” says George. That means if your shield is too thin, the astronauts behind it will be blasted with a surprisingly large dose of radiation. 



Then you have the sun. It may sustain life on Earth, but without our planet’s thick atmosphere and magnetic bubble to get in its way, moonwalkers will occasionally be blasted by one of its paroxysms: a solar flare (a burst of diverse types of radiation) or a coronal mass ejection (volleys of magnetized plasma). “During Apollo, they knew that if a large solar flare occurred while the crew was on the moon, there would be no way to keep them alive,” says Metzger. The crew could have developed acute radiation sickness and perished in a matter of days.



The way to survive a powerful solar flare or coronal mass ejection is straightforward: “Get back inside a habitat where there’s more shielding,” says George—preferably a dedicated, highly shielded “storm shelter,” essentially a thick-walled bunker. The issue is that astronauts might be outside the base, driving a rover many miles away. Coronal mass ejections take hours to days to reach the vicinity of the Earth-moon system, but solar flares can do so in under an hour. And scientists can’t yet model the sun well enough to give much advance notice. “All of the capability to forecast solar storms is kind of like where weather forecasting [was] … in the ’50s and ’60s,” says George.



As for those punchy galactic cosmic rays, the only way to avoid them would be to put a lot of stuff—lunar rocks, possibly—between the astronauts and the sky. “Build habitat modules underground,” says Chris Dreyer, director of engineering at the Center for Space Resources at the Colorado School of Mines. One option: Burrow living quarters into lava tubes, the naturally hollowed-­out volcanic tunnels created by molten rock eons ago. At this point, NASA hasn’t mentioned any plans to make its moon base subterranean, but it may need to if it wants to end up with a small lunar city.







Radiation limits the time astronauts can spend on the lunar surface over their entire life—it can total around two years max, experts estimate, before the health risk becomes too high. Unfortunately, that’s not all space will throw at them. When the Artemis II astronauts swung around the far side of the moon earlier this year, they saw curious flashes light up the silvery land below. These were the explosive deaths of small meteoroids punching into the lunar surface.



Earth is naturally protected from smaller space rocks, up to around 50 feet in diameter: They burn up inconsequentially in the atmosphere. “You don’t have that option on the moon,” says Philip Lubin, a physicist and planetary defense researcher at the University of California, Santa Barbara. articles.title: The ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests
articles.summary: In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like canopies of mature growth. articles.full_text:
In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like canopies of mature growth. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, oversees this sequence of plots across the Barro Colorado Nature Monument, some of which date as far back as the 19th century. Not one of the trees she surveys was planted by human hands. She maps, measures, and tracks each trunk that emerges, revealing how waves of tree life rise from bare earth. 



Tropical forests like these are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. As part of an international network of researchers, Dent is deciphering the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has built a body of evidence that such large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide. 





Few places are better to demonstrate this than Barro Colorado, a reserve covering the forested peninsulas and islands that formed when construction of the Panama Canal flooded the area in 1914. Under the management of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, generations of ecologists have amassed more than a century of records. 



That means Dent can trace why some plots rebound after clear-cutting for farming and forestry while others falter. Fruit-eating animals—including spider monkeys, bats, and parrots—are responsible for planting more than 70% of trees in tropical forests, and Dent’s dataset can tell which built each patch of trees by depositing seeds in their nutrient-rich droppings. Many of these creatures worked together to plant a diverse 70-year-old patch whose canopy is approaching the stunning structure and richness of an ancient jungle. In contrast, a patch of similar age populated by narrow trunks of a single long-lived species, Gustavia superba, hints that tropical rodents called agoutis are more or less the sole animal architects behind this more homogeneous forest. 



The data she collects helps write a playbook for when to let ecosystems regenerate and when to give them a helping hand. One 2024 estimate in Nature found that some 215 million hectares of forest worldwide (an area larger than Mexico) could regenerate naturally. “Tropical forests are underpinned by this massive network of interactions,” Dent says—interactions between life-forms like the fungi that help trees take up nutrients, as well as pollinators and seed-distributors. Supporting those relationships is key to growing forests that lock up carbon and help sustain local communities and wildlife. 



Filling in the gaps



Just over a decade ago, as the landmark Paris Agreement was being codified in 2015, forest recovery seized global attention as a solution to the climate crisis. Global leaders rallied behind plans to regrow a trillion trees, after the ecologist Thomas Crowther highlighted their potential to capture a decade’s worth of global carbon emissions. But the biggest question has lingered: How, exactly, do you regrow two trees for every star in the Milky Way?



While startups have proposed seed-spraying drones and nutrient-coated seed bombs, Dent has spent two decades studying what happens when we let forests rebuild themselves. As a PhD student around the turn of the millennium, she researched old-growth forests in northern Borneo but felt hopeless watching entire landscapes felled for palm oil plantations. Rather than despair, she turned to restoration. Then, as a postdoc in 2005, she joined Panama’s Prorena, a joint initiative between the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute and the Yale School of Forestry and Environmental Studies, which aimed at determining how best to establish diverse native forests on clear-cut land.



Back then, secondary forests—ones that grow naturally after the original forest was lost—had been “a bit of a niche research area,” Dent says. But as farming and human infrastructure have driven deforestation, resurgent forests now account for some 70% of all tropical canopies. Prorena initially followed the usual playbook of transplanting nursery trees to rangelands, but Dent began to question whether planting was necessary. In 2009, she published an encouraging paper showing that animal populations rebound quickly as forests naturally regrow.



In 2010, she began working in Barro Colorado on the plots established by the pioneering American ecologist Julie Denslow. In 1994, Denslow identified plots that had been regenerating naturally for 20 to 100 years, and Dent would add younger ones to continue the sequence. 





The site provides not just general data on forest regrowth but in-depth demographic information over time, says Robin Chazdon, a professor emeritus of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Connecticut who collaborated with Denslow when she established the plots. “It tells you more about the actual processes that are happening in the site,” she says. 



For example, previous research had shown that fast-growing “pioneer trees,” the first to thrive in the damaged land, are eventually overtaken by larger carbon-storing trees. Dent’s research helped fill in gaps about the mechanics of how this happens—or doesn’t happen—in individual cases. In the Gustavia-dominated patch, for instance, stubborn grasses planted by cattle ranchers smothered most other trees before they could take root. These trees can hang around, crowding out the light, for 150 years, blocking the second wave of large-trunked trees. 



To plant or not to plant



Dent found herself well placed for the massive influx of interest in reforestation that began in 2015. She’d already become a principal investigator for 2ndFor, an international research network aiming to learn how best to manage secondary forests. Using data gathered from the Barro Colorado plots, the team authored a 2016 paper in Nature showing that a hectare of naturally regenerated secondary forest can capture 11 times as much carbon each year as an old-growth one, with young trees absorbing it quickly as they compete to grow toward the sun. 



Then, in a 2022 study published by the Royal Society, Dent and colleagues showed that locations such as Barro Colorado are among the best-case scenarios for what can be achieved without planting a single seed. Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which help tree cover regain old-growth levels of richness and abundance within a few decades. Using data from Panama and Brazil, Dent published a follow-up in 2024 showing that plots with as little as 35% of tree cover can regenerate as forest. 



“Having these long-term mapped forest plots is really valuable,” says Liza Comita, a professor of tropical forest ecology at Yale University, who is collaborating with Dent on projects that translate her findings into action. “It provides this really nice research infrastructure where you can build projects on top of that.” 



In Panama, Dent works with nonprofits and carbon-crediting schemes to fast-track recovery. They’ve mapped corridors to reconnect forest fragments and made plans to reintroduce animals in “silent forests” that have lost much of their wildlife. They’re also working to replant tree species that can accelerate growth—what Comita calls assisted natural regeneration. Leaving plots alone may seem like the simpler option, but it can’t be done everywhere, says Dent. Many sites are too degraded. 




Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which helps tree cover regain old-growth ­levels of richness.




The two are working with the London-based carbon-crediting startup Ponterra to develop solutions for a region of southern Panama where remnant forests line the edges of abandoned ranches. Such sites almost always need some intervention, Comita explains. Many demand hands-on actions, such as enrichment planting. 



Today, the questions projects like Ponterra are asking are closer to her own research, says Dent. For instance, they want to understand if solitary standing trees, often left by ranchers to shade cows, help sites regenerate faster. Those insights can help Ponterra sell high-quality credits and avoid the embarrassing pitfalls that can lead fresh plantations to literally go up in smoke. While credits can be bought for as little as $5 per metric ton, corporate giants such as Microsoft—one of Ponterra’s clients—have paid more than 10 times as much for high-quality removal.



There are plenty of places where a level of natural regeneration can work well. So far, millions of hectares of rainforest are naturally regenerating in Brazil, according to the Brazilian Restoration and Reforestation Observatory. Still, Dent is mystified as to why the people in charge of large-scale projects continue to think the best solution is the one that imposes humans’ will on the landscape. 



The conversation may be shifting. As droughts hit Latin America, policymakers and carbon creditors might be forced to face the shortcomings of cookie-cutter plantations. “You have much reduced resilience in the system when it comes to extreme events like droughts or floods or extreme heat or pathogens,” Dent says. The coming year’s “mega El Niño” could be a moment of reckoning, she says: “I think there’s an increasing recognition that we can’t just plant trees. We have to rebuild a system.” 



Matthew Ponsford is a freelance reporter based in London.

articles.full_text:
Python 3.15 is here! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11.
First, some highlights from Python 3.15.
Explicit lazy imports
I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810. These let you import modules like so:
lazy import json
lazy from pathlib import Path
The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows.
My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost.
Unpacking in comprehensions
The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation:
lists = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]
[*L for L in lists]
# [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
# equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L]

sets = [{1, 2}, {2, 3}, {3, 4}]
{*s for s in sets}
# {1, 2, 3, 4}
# equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s}

dicts = [{'a': 1}, {'b': 2}, {'a': 3}]
{**d for d in dicts}
# {'a': 3, 'b': 2}
# equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()}
PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448, which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015.
A sampling profiler
Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing, and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling.
Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first.
I've previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library.
If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS):
sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234
Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this:

It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this, and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI.
3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14
Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase.
Miguel's explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories.
Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv
I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release:
uv self update
Then I installed the stable 3.15 release:
uv python install 3.15
And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version:
uv python pin --global 3.15
Now the following reports 3.15 as the version:
uv run python --version
I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install. I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this:
uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15
Then I can confirm the version like this:
datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq
Highlights from Python 3.11
The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported.
My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11.
Here's the What's new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available!
Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio. 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout(), and several more new features.
datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc.
Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including:


setlimit() and getlimit() expose a mechanism for setting SQLite runtime limits from Python.

create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with step(), value(), inverse(), and finalize() methods.

blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large BLOB binary values stored in a SQLite row.
You can now call set_authorizer(None) to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this!

Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python's typing system.
I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround.
I've also updated my click-app, datasette-plugin, python-lib, and llm-plugin cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15.

articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03225-6Better career support and more funding stability is needed to retain this invaluable group of scientists.

Gordon W. Stewart is an emeritus professor of experimental medicine and former director of the UCL MB–PhD programme, Division of Medicine, University College London, London, UK.
Áine Burns is a professor of postgraduate medical education and nephrology and former director of the UCL MB–PhD programme, Royal Free Hospital, London, UK.
Reza Motallebzadeh is a professor of renal transplantation and director of the UCL MB–PhD programme in the Department of Surgical Biotechnology, University College London, UK.
Medical doctors who also do research are an increasingly rare breed. Physician-scientists made up nearly 5% of the US medical workforce in the 1980s; today, that figure is closer to 1.5%1. In the United Kingdom, the proportion of senior doctors working as academics fell from almost 5% in 2009 to roughly 3% in 2025 (see ‘Physician-scientists on the ropes’), with the number of physician-scientists under the age of 36 plunging by a whopping 25% between 2024 and 2025 (see go.nature.com/4ygjfev). In Japan, 2.1% of all doctors were physician-scientists in 1996; this proportion dropped to 1.6% in 2016. Moreover, the number of physician-scientists aged 39 or younger halved in the same period2.
Underlying the decline is an inability to retain young physician-scientists at a high enough rate to replace senior professionals as they retire. Around the world, clinical academics describe funding instability and a lack of career support as barriers to staying in their posts3–6. In the United States, according to a survey posted on the preprint website medRxiv, more than half of early-career physician-scientists are considering quitting their academic duties to pursue a purely clinical career7. That’s markedly higher than the 31% of US physicians who report considering leaving their current post within two years.
This trend is alarming because physician-scientists are hugely valuable for health-care research. Their expertise makes them ideally placed to pioneer advances in translational medicine, formulate and run medical trials to improve clinical practice, and drive economic growth. More than one-third of the Nobel Prizes in Physiology or Medicine and Lasker Awards for basic science have been awarded to physician-scientists8.
South Korea offers a glimpse of what is at stake. The number of medical research papers it published was already declining — probably owing to funding cuts — when, in 2024, mass resignations by resident physicians forced physician-scientists to abandon research to cover clinical duties9. That year, publications fell by 12%, roughly double the decline in the previous year, presumably in part because of the lack of papers from physician-scientists.
Our own experiences have further convinced us of the value of this group. Two of us (R.M. and R.B.) currently lead the University College London MB–PhD programme, which has run since 1994. It enables undergraduate medical students to undertake a PhD in scientific research, typically between their fourth and fifth years — one of several routes to becoming a physician-scientist. Papers authored by our cohort of 131 graduates from the programme between 1994 and 2026 received about three times as many citations each per year as did comparable papers in related fields10.
These results are just a snapshot from a small group, and there are many factors that could contribute to the cohort’s high performance. However, we think that they highlight the importance of the blended expertise that defines physician-scientists.
That expertise is now eroding around the world. Governments, funders, universities and others must take urgent steps to stop the decline.
Reasons for the drop-off
In many countries, medical graduates are matched to their first postgraduate positions by centralized, algorithmic systems built for all physicians. These systems do not always consider research potential. In England, for instance, two-thirds of posts historically reserved for aspiring physician-scientists are now allocated by an algorithm that does not take into account publication record11. When recruitment processes consider research, they often reward the quantity of a candidate’s research output rather than quality.
There’s no guarantee that the location to which a physician-scientist is recruited will have an academic department nearby where they can pursue their research area of interest. Schemes implemented in countries such as the United Kingdom, Australia and Canada deliberately post doctors to under-served regions. This is a sensible response to genuine workforce shortages, but one that can inadvertently displace physician-scientists far away from the infrastructure that their research depends on.
Next, there’s a lack of career support. Once a physician-scientist is in a post, health systems often fail to dedicate time and support for research. They might be awarded protected research time on paper but spend it covering rota gaps or absorbing high clinical workloads. One UK survey found that more than 50% of physicians reported a lack of protected research time in their job plans12. Mentoring is often lacking13, and when it’s available, it might not come from people who understand both the clinical and scientific sides of the job.
Pay for physician-scientists often falls short of that for equivalent, purely clinical posts. In the United States, for example, academic physicians are compensated, on average, about US$50,000 less per year than are conventional hospital doctors (see go.nature.com/4y9anls). The same problem occurs across Europe3. And in England, although a pay premium recognizes physicians who combine research with clinical training, some people are ineligible — notably, those who receive a PhD before graduating in medicine.
Underpinning all of these challenges is funding instability, in both medicine and research. In 2025, US federal funding cuts forced universities to rescind offers already made to incoming physician–PhD (MD–PhD) students. The Canadian Institutes of Health Research announced that it would revoke funding for its national MD–PhD training programme in 2015 and has yet to replace it. In the past few years, research funding has been cut in countries including Argentina and the Netherlands14, resulting in fewer grants and fewer researchers.
Rebuild the workforce
A coordinated effort from governments, funders, health systems, universities and physician-scientists is needed to retain more people in this profession.
Health and science ministries should track how many doctors at each career stage enter fundamental or clinical research, remain active or leave. They should publish where and why attrition occurs. This will let ministries target interventions at the points at which talent is lost and assess whether reforms are working.
