The 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel has been awarded to economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford for their research on how to stabilize an economy to avoid socially and economically damaging fluctuations in inflation, growth and employment.
The work, in the words of the prize awarding committee, “generated a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy and [is] now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world”.
“This is an excellent prize, honouring two superb and highly influential economists,” says economist John Cochrane of the Hoover Institution, a thinktank based at Stanford University. Olivier Blanchard, formerly chief economist at the International Monetary Fund, says the laureates have “dramatically changed the conduct of monetary policy”.
According to Cochrane, there were “a dozen plausible contenders at least” to share a prize in this field. “I would hate to be the Nobel Prize committee deciding which two or three to recognize”, he says, but “Hall and Woodford were top contenders on anyone’s list”.
Speaking by phone during the prize announcement, Woodford said he was “elated” by the award. He added that his theory was intended not just to guide policy but also to help governments explain to the public why they make economic interventions in the way they do, “to talk to people about why the things that are being done are being done”.
“Together, Hall’s and Woodford’s contributions amount to a new foundation for the theory of macroeconomic fluctuations”, say the Nobel committee, “allowing us to obtain a deeper understanding of the sources and propagation mechanisms behind recessions and booms.”
The return of Keynes
The work of the two laureates, who share the prize of 12 million Swedish kronor (around $1.2 million), builds on the ideas of the twentieth century British economist John Maynard Keynes.
Keynes argued that governments need to intervene on a big scale in times of economic instability to avoid crashes and mass unemployment as happened in the Great Depression of the 1930s. Market forces alone cannot give an economy sufficient agility to respond to such crises, he contended in books such as How to Pay for the War, published just after Britain had declared war against Nazi Germany (Macmillan, 1940).
Keynes’ ideas became highly influential from the mid-20th-century onwards. They were relevant as recently as the COVID-19 pandemic when governments around the world funded businesses so they could retain their staff during lockdowns. But these ideas did not prevent the rollercoaster of economic boom and bust, evident for example in the oil crisis of the 1970s, and the financial crisis of 2008.
Hall and Woodford effect
Hall and Woodford’s work has helped to explain what was missing in Keynes’ macroeconomic picture – the study of the economy as a whole – by diving deep into the microeconomic perspective, which considers how decisions made by individual businesses and households affect prices, earnings, and spending.
Hall, based at Stanford University in California, recognized that people’s decisions about consumption depend not just on quantifiable factors such as earnings but on what Keynes himself called “animal spirits”: psychological factors that drive economic choices, in this case expectations about the future.
In two key papers, in 1978 and in 1982, Hall showed that it is possible to estimate the proportion of spenders who take a rational view of how they think future monetary and fiscal policies might change, as well asthose who in contrast make their decisions about consumption based only on an immediate, gloomy prospect of having no savings or access to borrowing. In effect, this amounts to estimating the proportions of the population that are forward-looking in their spending decisions and that are not. Hall validated his predictions against real-world data on consumption.
Woodford, based at Columbia University in New York, built on such work about expectations to create a 'New Keynesian' microeconomic theory, which culminated in his book Interest and Prices: Foundations of a Theory of Monetary Policy (Princeton University Press, 2003).

What does a PhD pay? Data reveal huge gaps across Europe
Earnings come in a combination of scholarships and salaries and vary widely between countries, an analysis by international federation Eurodoc reveals.
How much do PhD students earn? The first comprehensive overview of PhD income shows vast imbalances across much of Europe1.
The report, which investigated the earnings of first-year doctoral candidates in 2024–25 across 26 countries, was published by the European Council of Doctoral Candidates and Junior Researchers (Eurodoc) in September.
“Collecting comparative data on remuneration across Europe is notoriously difficult,” says Norbert Bencze, one of the authors of the report and president of Eurodoc — an international federation based in Brussels that represents early-career researchers and doctoral candidates across Europe. “Our aim is to draw attention to the disparities, and to encourage more data collection.”
But Estonia has shown that it is possible to buck that trend, Saugmann adds. A 2022 doctoral education reform replaced a student stipend of around €8,000 (about US$9,000) a year with a guaranteed salary of about 2.5 times that amount, boosting applications for doctoral positions, as well as connections to industry, she says.
Accounting complexities
Remuneration schemes can be difficult to compare, says Bencze. Some doctoral candidates are employed with salaries, others are on scholarships and some have mixed arrangements. The cost of living, which differs widely between places, also matters.
For paid employment, income is taxed, so individuals will take home a much lower figure — but they might receive compensations such as pension entitlements and parental leave. By contrast, scholarship money is generally exempt from taxation, but might not come with any other benefits.

An ambiguous instruction caused the chatbot to send three e-mails from Ying Zhao’s connected account. The incident advanced Zhao’s project, but showed that chatbots need limits.
I was trying to rescue a plan for a perspective article after two journals had declined it. My take-away was that my concept was not enough: the project needed evidence. I decided to use an artificial-intelligence tool to help with brainstorming.
I study soil hydrology — how water moves through soils and landscapes, shaping erosion, plant growth and ecological recovery. I wanted to investigate landscape restoration on China’s Loess Plateau, so I asked OpenAI’s ChatGPT chatbot to help me redesign my perspective as a data-driven study.
For several hours, ChatGPT did what I expected it to. It searched for relevant journal papers online and analysed the articles and draft files that I supplied it with to help me develop a research plan. It found that other teams had already documented some water- and sediment-related changes that I had thought were fresh, which forced me to narrow my aims. The chatbot also provided recommendations about what data to include in my modelling and how best to incorporate published statistical benchmarks.
Then, the project hit a snag. I needed published maps and data but had difficulty retrieving them. And in some cases, I needed extra metadata. ChatGPT identified the teams behind several data sets relevant to my work and drafted requests tailored to specific researchers for the information I needed. I kept replying to the chatbot with ‘Please continue’ in Chinese. To me, that meant continuing the search and analysis processes that it had been doing so far. But I had not explicitly defined the limits of that instruction. I was impressed by the speed at which the model could complete tasks and, in hindsight, had stopped asking enough questions about what the chatbot’s planned steps involved.
Eventually, the model crossed a concerning boundary. I was using the ChatGPT interface and had connected my e-mail account to it. The model used that access to e-mail five researchers to request their original data sets — a step that I had not anticipated and which ChatGPT had not told me it would do. Each message explained my scientific question, requested specific data and metadata and attached a two-page pre-analysis summary. I learnt that ChatGPT had done this only when it reported in our chat that it had sent the messages.
The responses that I received to the e-mails were helpful. One researcher provided a geospatial data set that mapped more than 50,000 sediment-accumulation areas behind check dams — barriers that slow run-off and retain sediment upstream — on the Loess Plateau. A second researcher confirmed that a multi-gigabyte archive was public, offered to prepare a smaller subset of the data and suggested that we discuss collaboration. A third professor who was away on fieldwork at the time welcomed the message and said that he would follow up after returning. The information that I was given in these e-mails allowed me to advance the project. But the useful outcomes of ChatGPT’s behaviour do not negate the fact that the actions it took were unauthorized.
The boundary I missed
It would be easy to say that the chatbot had ‘gone rogue’, but that would obscure my share of the responsibility. I had connected ChatGPT to my e-mail account, had repeatedly used an open-ended instruction and had never required the model to distinguish between analysis and drafting done inside the research workspace and external actions taken in my name. My mistake was assuming that the scope of ‘continue’ was obvious.
This experience has taught me to make a distinction between what an AI tool can do and what it should do: capability is not permission. Giving ChatGPT access to my e-mail account was not synonymous with giving it permission to send those messages. Its report afterwards made me aware of its behaviour, but transparency after the fact is not a substitute for authorization beforehand.

articles.title: Antiviral immunity via telomerase-like reverse transcription in bacteria
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11250-8Antiviral immunity via telomerase-like reverse transcription in bacteria
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Defense-associated reverse transcriptases (DRTs) employ diverse and distinctive mechanisms of cDNA synthesis to protect bacteria against viral infection1.
However, the functions and mechanisms of many DRTs remain unknown2.
Here we identify a new antiviral defense system, DRT10, that associates with a noncoding RNA (ncRNA) to catalyze processive, protein-primed synthesis of tandem-repeat DNA.
Reverse transcription is templated by a defined ncRNA region with a characteristic sequence pattern and template boundary elements, both of which are conserved and essential for DNA repeat addition.
Cryo-EM reconstructions reveal an unanticipated 2:1 architecture, wherein two RT monomers bind opposite sides of a pseudo-symmetric ncRNA.
Biochemical experiments further demonstrate that each RT monomer reverse transcribes the template encoded on its respective side of the ncRNA, but only one generates the long repetitive product, whose template is defined by the distance between two flanking stem-loop anchors.
This mode of iterative, boundary-delimited cDNA synthesis exhibits direct parallels to the mechanism of telomeric repeat addition by eukaryotic telomerase, and phylogenetic analyses of RTs across domains of life place telomerase in a monophyletic clade with the DRT family, suggesting a common origin for their DNA polymerization activities.
Together with earlier studies of DRT2, DRT3, and DRT93–5, our findings identify a conserved mechanistic logic underlying RNA-templated DNA repeat addition across diverse DRTs, despite vastly different architectural solutions, and expand the repertoire of reverse transcription-based strategies for antiviral immunity in bacteria.

articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03227-4Concerns about privacy, reproducibility and cost are prompting scientists to use models on their computers rather than in the cloud.

When he wants to scratch an intellectual itch, Ian Gaudet does what people are increasingly doing on the Internet: he asks a chatbot. But when it comes to his research data, Gaudet, a neuroscientist at Florida Atlantic University in Boca Raton, prefers to stay offline. “I do not want Claude to start telling people my research results,” he explains.
Cloud-based large language models (LLMs), such as those underlying the chatbots Claude (Anthropic), Gemini (Google) and ChatGPT (OpenAI), represent the cutting edge of artificial-intelligence performance. However, these systems might use what is typed into them for training purposes. For researchers such as Gaudet, state-of-the-art performance isn’t worth the risk to data protection, reproducibility or budgets. Instead, they turn to a growing collection of tools, such as Ollama and LM Studio, that enable researchers to download LLMs to their computer and use them offline.
These programs can help researchers to sort and query their own literature libraries to gather insights, for instance. But two fresh barriers have replaced the programming and set-up issues that once kept researchers from using them: the hardware needed to run them has become much more expensive, and the tools’ output still requires scrutiny to assess its veracity.
Going local
Ask researchers why they want to run an AI model on their desktop rather than in the cloud, and the answer almost always starts with data. Eric Böhnisch-Volkmann, president of DEVONtechnologies in Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, hears it constantly from users of the firm’s document-management software DEVONthink, which integrates LLMs.
“Medical records is one thing, lawsuits is one other thing, research is another,” he says. “They just want to keep their hands on [their data] and not give it to someone else they don’t trust.”
Privacy concerns are well founded. A 2025 analysis found that the six AI developers studied — Amazon, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI — trained their models on users’ input data by default (J. King et al. Preprint at arXiv https://doi.org/g967b4; 2025).
Ahmed Farooq, a computer scientist at Tampere University in Finland, built a local system called TAUCHI-GPT, so that papers, reports and study data protected under the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation could be searched without leaving the university’s network.
Reproducibility is another benefit: cloud-based AI providers update their models without notice, so a query that works today might return different results next month. Casey Greene, a biomedical informatician at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine in Aurora, notes that if a local model converts his documents into a searchable index using the same settings each time, the results will always be identical. “If you want to use that for a scientific workflow, being able to know that is important,” he says.
Another benefit of local LLMs is economic. Jayashree Kalpathy-Cramer, who leads ophthalmology AI research at Anschutz, used Qwen (developed by Alibaba Cloud) and NVIDIA Nemotron through Ollama to index a decade’s worth of open-access publications on her machines. The corpus is public, so she could send it to a remote, commercial AI system. But local inference is free, and that changes how she works. Her system sends a daily briefing to her department’s chair highlighting new papers worth reading. The same query is run through three or four AI models, before another model reconciles the outputs, and every summarized finding is checked against the passage it came from. Because all of the field’s records sit in one searchable index, she can cluster them, map them and ask the LLM where any research gaps are.
The search for meaning
Preliminary findings of a survey by Wiley, a scientific publisher in Hoboken, New Jersey, indicate that 68% of some 2,400 researchers worldwide had used AI for literature searches or reviews (see go.nature.com/4rpuvwj). The tasks that were embraced fastest include reviewing large collections of studies, monitoring the latest publications and assisting with writing. Those are jobs that local models already do well, says Kalpathy-Cramer.
Greene built a local database of embeddings — numerical representations of each document’s overall meaning — to process the public abstracts of grants awarded to his university. When a federal-funding call for proposals in HIV research came through, he searched his database for potential collaborators. A keyword search for HIV highlighted a group researching the virus. But a semantic search of the same database, which looks at meaning rather than exact words, also came up with a researcher whose grants did not mention HIV in the title but who studied antiretroviral therapies, he says. He then asked that researcher about collaborating.
Dmitrijs Lvovs, a bioinformatician at the Institute for Genome Sciences at the University of Maryland School of Medicine in Baltimore, uses a computational pipeline to analyse spatial data from tumour tissue, producing hundreds of tables containing gene activity data, cell-type interaction information and records of treatment responses. To make sense of those data, he and his colleagues paste them into Microsoft Copilot, the cloud-based AI service that their university provides. The tool then searches the published literature and suggests what any patterns might mean. But Lvovs wants to bring that step in-house. So, he started using a tool called llmize to feed the tables into Google Gemma 4 through Ollama, in a fully offline environment.
Because the model is not connected to the Internet, Gemma cannot search the literature in the way that Copilot can. But the tables represent people’s data, and Lvovs would rather accept a ‘weaker’ model than send such data sets to the cloud. Even if study participants have given their consent for data collection, “it feels wrong to be concentrating all that data in the hands of a few companies”, he says.
Getting started
In the world of LLMs, ‘weaker’ is a moving target, and the gap between local and cloud-based models is shrinking fast, Lvovs says. “The competition is now more about the harness, the actual program that uses the model as a back end, not the model itself.”
